economics.title: From probability to approval: choose the threshold economically
economics.text:
From probability to approval: choose the threshold economically

 Assume a simplified loss table per application:

            Decision error                                        Example cost                                           Why
            Approve a borrower who defaults                             $4,000           principal loss, servicing, collections
            Decline a borrower who would repay                            $450    lost contribution margin and relationship
            Manual review                                                  $18                        analyst time and delay


 Threshold exercise
 For thresholds t ∈ {0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30}, calculate:

                                            Expected cost(t) = 4000 F N (t) + 450 F P (t) + 18 Nreview (t)

 Select the operating point using validation data, then report one untouched test result.

 Watch for: A threshold optimized on one economic cycle may fail when loss rates, funding costs, or
 applicant mix change.

economics.title: How to evaluate tree models honestly
economics.text:
How to evaluate tree models honestly


1. Compare against the rule baseline and logistic regression.
2. Tune depth and minimum leaf size on validation data.
3. Measure performance at the actual review capacity: precision@500, not only global AUC.
4. Check probability calibration; tree ensembles can rank well while overstating confidence.
5. Test slices: new customers, high-value transactions, device changes, and rare merchants.

 Feature importance is not causality
 Impurity-based importance can favor continuous or high-cardinality features. Use permutation tests,
 stability checks, and domain review before drawing conclusions.

Measure performance at the actual review capacity: precision@500, not only global AUC. 4. Check probability calibration; tree ensembles can rank well while overstating confidence. 5. Test slices: new customers, high-value transactions, device changes, and rare merchants.

economics.title: How to evaluate clustering when there is no target label
economics.text:
How to evaluate clustering when there is no target label



1. Internal quality: silhouette, within-cluster dispersion, separation.
2. Stability: rerun with new samples, seeds, and time windows. Do the same segments reappear?
3. Interpretability: can analysts describe each group with observed behavior rather than
   stereotypes?
4. Actionability: does the segment support a different offer, service path, or risk treatment?
5. Outcome validation: after deployment, do interventions produce different measurable results by
   segment?

 A common failure
 Teams select k from a chart, name clusters with marketing language, and never test whether the
 segments improve a decision.

Financial problem: how do we find a fraud pattern we have never
 labeled?


    Financial problem

 Supervised fraud models learn known patterns from labeled outcomes. Anomaly detection searches

   means fraudulent.

economics.title: Evaluation without pretending labels do not matter
economics.text:
Evaluation without pretending labels do not matter



1. Use later-confirmed outcomes or analyst adjudication to estimate precision@k.
2. Track how many novel cases were found beyond existing rules.
3. Measure review burden: alerts per analyst, time per case, and repeat false positives.
4. Evaluate by customer and merchant slices, not only overall.
5. Backtest chronologically; anomaly definitions drift as products and behavior change.

 Common failure
 The model rediscovers “large transaction” and floods analysts with wealthy customers, travel,
 payroll events, or seasonal activity.
 Required artifact: Top-alert review table with reason codes and analyst disposition.

economics.text:

   Decision to make: Choose the narrowest task that solves the financial problem. Do not use
   generation when a tested classifier is enough.

economics.title: How to evaluate a financial language classifier
economics.text:
How to evaluate a financial language classifier



1. Use an in-domain labeled test set, not generic movie reviews or social media.
2. Report per-class precision and recall; neutral often dominates.
3. Review disagreement cases where experts themselves differ.
4. Test slices: sectors, document types, sentence length, negation, and dates.
5. Monitor label distribution and confidence drift after deployment.

 A high confidence score is not a guarantee
 Neural classifiers can be confidently wrong under domain shift. Calibrate or threshold confidence
 only after testing on representative data.
 Required artifact: Confusion matrix, challenge set, and documented abstention threshold.

economics.title: The real risk is input sensitivity
economics.text:
The real risk is input sensitivity



▶ Expected returns are estimated with large error.
▶ Correlations change during stress, often when diversification is needed most.
▶ Small input changes can create large allocation changes.
▶ Unconstrained solutions may concentrate in assets with optimistic estimates.

 Required sensitivity test
 Perturb each expected return by ±1% and each correlation by ±0.10. Report whether the
 recommended portfolio remains recognizable.
 Required artifact: Equal-weight comparison, sensitivity analysis, turnover estimate, and
 documented constraints.

economics.title: How to evaluate reinforcement learning
economics.text:
How to evaluate reinforcement learning



1. Compare against TWAP, VWAP, and simple adaptive policies.
2. Run many random seeds; report distributions, not one lucky trajectory.
3. Evaluate out of sample across volatility and liquidity regimes.
4. Check constraint violations and incomplete orders explicitly.
5. Stress the simulator and test for reward hacking.
6. Use shadow mode before any live action.
 Primary metric: Implementation shortfall, tail slippage, completion rate, and constraint violations.
 Required artifact: Baseline comparison, reward specification, stress scenarios, and trace of
 decisions.

code.text:
Working example: a tiny execution agent


  import numpy as np
  rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
  T, inventory0, actions = 10, 10, np.array([0,1,2])
                                                                                                                       Important
  Q = np.zeros((T+1, inventory0+1, len(actions)))
  alpha, gamma, eps = .15, .95, .20                                                                                    This is a teaching
  for episode in range(8000):                                                                                          environment, not a
      inv = inventory0
      for t in range(T):                                                                                               market model. Students
          valid = np.where(actions <= inv)[0]
          a_idx = rng.choice(valid) if rng.random() < eps else valid[np.argmax(Q[t,inv,valid])]                        should inspect how the
          qty = actions[a_idx]
          impact = .08 * qty**2                                                                                        policy changes when:
          price_risk = rng.normal(0, .10) * inv
          next_inv = inv - qty
          reward = -(impact + price_risk)
                                                                                                                       ▶ impact rises,
          if t == T-1: reward -= 5.0 * next_inv # incomplete penalty
          next_valid = np.where(actions <= next_inv)[0]                                                                ▶ penalty rises,
          future = 0 if t == T-1 else Q[t+1,next_inv,next_valid].max()
          Q[t,inv,a_idx] += alpha * (reward + gamma*future - Q[t,inv,a_idx])
          inv = next_inv
                                                                                                                       ▶ volatility rises.
  policy, inv = [], inventory0
  for t in range(T):
      valid = np.where(actions <= inv)[0]
      qty = actions[valid[np.argmax(Q[t,inv,valid])]]
      policy.append(qty); inv -= qty
  print("illustrative actions:", policy, "remaining:", inv)

problem.title: Financial problem: how much reserve is enough?
problem.text:
Financial problem: how much reserve is enough?



    Financial problem
    A lender holds a portfolio of 1,000 loans. It knows average default probability and loss given
    default, but management needs the full loss distribution–especially the tail.


 A point estimate is not enough
 Expected loss supports pricing and provisioning. Capital and contingency planning require plausible
 severe outcomes and their probability.

   Decision to make: Simulate many coherent scenarios, then inspect the distribution of losses
   rather than one “most likely” number.

economics.title: How to validate a simulation
economics.text:
How to validate a simulation


1. Verify the code on a case with a known analytical answer.
2. Check convergence: do key quantiles stabilize as runs increase?
3. Stress assumptions one at a time and together.
4. Backtest distributions where enough history exists.
5. Separate parameter uncertainty from random scenario variation.
6. Report assumptions beside every result.

 False precision
 “The 99th percentile loss is $327,418” is misleading if PD, LGD, and correlation are rough
 estimates. Report sensible ranges and sensitivity.
 Required artifact: Assumption register, convergence plot, sensitivity table, and tail-loss summary.

code.title: Working example: correlated loan losses
code.text:
Working example: correlated loan losses



  import numpy as np
  from scipy.stats import norm
  rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
                                                                                     Modify
  n_sims, n_loans = 5000, 1000                                                       ▶ Set ρ = 0.
  pd = np.full(n_loans, .025)
  ead = np.full(n_loans, 10000.0)
  lgd = np.full(n_loans, .45)
                                                                                     ▶ Double PD.
  rho = .12
                                                                                     ▶ Make LGD random.
  common = rng.normal(size=(n_sims, 1))
  idiosyncratic = rng.normal(size=(n_sims, n_loans))
  latent = np.sqrt(rho)*common + np.sqrt(1-rho)*idiosyncratic
                                                                                     ▶ Add sector factors.
  defaults = latent < norm.ppf(pd)
  loss = (defaults * ead * lgd).sum(axis=1)                                          Primary metric: Tail
  print("Expected loss:", loss.mean())
  print("95th percentile:", np.quantile(loss, .95))
                                                                                     quantiles and probability
  print("99th percentile:", np.quantile(loss, .99))
  print("P(loss > $200k):", (loss > 200000).mean())
                                                                                     of breaching a reserve.

slides.title: Confusion Matrix
slides.text:
Confusion Matrix

   M01 | Worked solution — Count the Four Outcomes

1. True positives: The 15 confirmed frauds among the flags give T P = 15.
2. False positives: F P = 50 − 15 = 35.
3. False negatives: F N = 20 − 15 = 5.
4. True negatives: There are 1,000 − 20 = 980 legitimate transactions, so
   T N = 980 − 35 = 945.
   Decision                                       Actually fraud                   Actually legitimate
   Flagged                                                   15                                    35
   Not flagged                                                 5                                  945
 Check: 15 + 35 + 5 + 945 = 1,000.

Decision Actually fraud Actually legitimate Flagged 15 35 Not flagged 5 945 Check: 15 + 35 + 5 + 945 = 1,000.

slides.title: Confusion Matrix
slides.text:
Confusion Matrix

   M01 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The detector finds 15 frauds, misses 5, interrupts 35 legitimate transactions, and correctly
 passes 945. These are counts at one chosen threshold, not probabilities.
 Why these steps matter
 The total number of flags includes false alarms. The total number of actual frauds includes
 missed fraud. Those two totals are usually different, which is why precision and recall require
 different denominators.

slides.title: Precision
slides.text:
Precision

   M04 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 B uses investigator time more efficiently: 80% of its alerts are genuine fraud, versus 30%

 What the answer means
 F1 = 0.429 summarizes the tradeoff; F2 = 0.577 places more emphasis on the stronger recall.

 detector has improved. It means the selected weighting gives more credit to the detector’s
 relatively high recall.

 higher capture may also interrupt more legitimate activity. In this small set, the denominators
 stay fixed, so changes in rates come entirely from changes in the flagged cases.

measures.question: rank
measures.financialInterpretation: ROC-AUC measures discrimination: whether risky cases tend to receive higher scores than safe cases, independent of one chosen threshold.
measures.workingExample: An ROC-AUC of 0.88 means that, for a randomly selected fraud and legitimate transaction, the fraud receives the higher score about 88% of the time. Gini = 2 × AUC − 1 = 2(0.88) − 1 = 0.76 Gini is a rescaled form of AUC commonly seen in credit-risk reporting.
measures.whatItMisses: AUC does not show whether probabilities are honest, whether the chosen threshold is profitable, or whether the top 200 alerts fit investigator capacity.

slides.title: Precision–Recall Curve
slides.text:
Precision–Recall Curve

   M11a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Reviewing six cases captures every fraud in this sample, but half the queue is legitimate. An
 empirical precision–recall curve can rise locally; precision does not necessarily fall at every
 additional rank.
 Why these steps matter
 Recall cannot decrease when the queue only expands, because caught frauds are not removed.
 Precision can rise or fall: its numerator and denominator change differently depending on
 whether the next case is fraud.

slides.title: Precision@K and Recall@K
slides.text:
Precision@K and Recall@K

   M12 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Expanding the queue lowers precision from 60% to 50% but increases fraud coverage from
 37.5% to 62.5%. The extra cases may be worth reviewing, but the institution must have
 capacity and a useful intervention. Higher precision alone is not the objective.
 Why these steps matter
 Use the difference in fraud discoveries to assess the added five reviews. Dividing incremental
 spending by all five frauds in the expanded queue would over-credit discoveries already made by
 the smaller queue.

Lift and Gain

   M13 | Class problem | 6 minutes — Compare With Random Review

 A batch contains 1,000 transactions and 20 frauds. The top 50 model-ranked transactions
 contain 15 frauds.
 Calculate:
1. Fraud prevalence and precision@50.
2. Lift@50: precision@50 divided by fraud prevalence.
3. Cumulative gain: the share of all frauds found in the top 50.
4. The expected number of frauds in a randomly selected set of 50 transactions.
 What percentage of the transaction population is reviewed? Explain what “15 times better”
 would mean here—and what it would not mean.
paragraphs: Lift and Gain
M13 | Class problem | 6 minutes — Compare With Random Review

A batch contains 1,000 transactions and 20 frauds. The top 50 model-ranked transactions contain 15 frauds. Calculate: 1. Fraud prevalence and precision@50. 2. Lift@50: precision@50 divided by fraud prevalence. 3. Cumulative gain: the share of all frauds found in the top 50. 4. The expected number of frauds in a randomly selected set of 50 transactions. What percentage of the transaction population is reviewed? Explain what “15 times better” would mean here—and what it would not mean.

slides.title: Lift and Gain
slides.text:
Lift and Gain

   M13 | Worked solution — Compare With Random Review

1. Prevalence: 20/1,000 = 2%.
2. Precision@50: 15/50 = 30%.
3. Lift: 30%/2% = 15.
4. Cumulative gain: 15/20 = 75% of all frauds.
5. Random-review expectation: 50(0.02) = 1 fraud, compared with the model’s 15 in this
   sample.
6. Population reviewed: 50/1,000 = 5%.
paragraphs: Lift and Gain
M13 | Worked solution — Compare With Random Review

1. Prevalence: 20/1,000 = 2%. 2. Precision@50: 15/50 = 30%. 3. Lift: 30%/2% = 15. 4. Cumulative gain: 15/20 = 75% of all frauds. 5. Random-review expectation: 50(0.02) = 1 fraud, compared with the model’s 15 in this sample. 6. Population reviewed: 50/1,000 = 5%.

slides.title: Lift and Gain
slides.text:
Lift and Gain

   M13 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Reviewing the top 5% captures 75% of frauds, with 15 times the fraud concentration of
 random review. This is not a 15-fold profit increase; fraud value, review cost, and the ability to
 prevent or recover losses remain separate questions.
 Why these steps matter
 A random sample will not necessarily contain exactly the expected fraud count. The lift
 comparison uses its expected concentration, not a claim that every random sample produces
 the same result.

slides.title: Calibration
slides.text:
Calibration

   M14 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The highest band understates observed risk in this sample, affecting the expected-loss
 calculation. The sample does not establish a permanent calibration error; uncertainty, time
 stability, and larger validation samples still matter.
 Why these steps matter
 Mean probability times group size equals the sum of individual probabilities, so it is appropriate
 for the expected count. Individual loans still default or do not default; a probability is evaluated
 by frequencies across cases, not by demanding that every single outcome match it exactly.

Brier Score

   M15 | Formula explained (1/1)

 Read it aloud: For each loan, subtract its actual binary outcome from its predicted probability,
 square that difference, add the squared differences, and divide by the number of loans.
 Squaring removes the sign and gives larger deviations more weight. Use probabilities as
 decimals, not whole-number percentages.
 This is the binary Brier-score convention with range 0 to 1. Lower is better on the same
 evaluated sample; zero requires every probability to match its realized label exactly.

 What the answer means
 The model has better average probability accuracy on these four loans than the constant
 baseline. 0.1125 is not an 11.25% default rate or dollar loss. One non-default on a 60%

Log Loss

   M16 | Formula explained (2/2)

 Why the logarithm matters
 A probability near 1 for the actual outcome gives a penalty near 0. A probability near 0 for the
 actual outcome gives a very large penalty.

 probability. Using the fraud probability directly would score the wrong event.

 An actual outcome assigned probability zero has unbounded log penalty; all supplied values here
 are strictly between 0 and 1.

slides.text:

   M19 | Worked solution — Compare Rates, Not Just Counts

1. Approval rates: A = 600/1,000 = 60%; B = 400/1,000 = 40%. B/A ratio
   = 40/60 = 0.667.
2. Repayment TPRs: A = 560/800 = 70%; B = 300/500 = 60%. Gap = 10 percentage
   points.
3. Non-repayers: A = 1,000 − 800 = 200; B = 1,000 − 500 = 500.
4. Non-repayers approved: A = 600 − 560 = 40; B = 400 − 300 = 100.
5. False-positive rates: A = 40/200 = 20%; B = 100/500 = 20%.

slides.title: Fairness Diagnostics
slides.text:
Fairness Diagnostics

   M19 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Approval rates and repayer capture differ even though both groups have the same FPR. These
 diagnostics identify differences that need investigation; they do not independently establish
 fairness, unfairness, or a legal conclusion. Outcome definitions, population differences, and
 uncertainty remain important.
 Why these steps matter
 The two groups have different repayment prevalences in the supplied benchmark. Equal FPR
 alone therefore does not imply equal approval rates or equal TPR. The arithmetic describes the
 pattern, not its cause or whether any decision is legally justified.

slides.text:
Scaled Forecast Errors

   M22 | Worked solution — Percentage of What?

1. Absolute test errors: [10, 10, 20, 10]; sum = 50; test MAE = 50/4 = 12.5.
2. Percentage errors: 10/100 = 10%; 10/120 = 8.333%; 20/80 = 25%; 10/150 = 6.667%.
                      M AP E = (10 + 8.333 + 25 + 6.667)/4 = 12.5%.
3. Aggregate scale: W AP E = 50/(100 + 120 + 80 + 150) = 11.11%.
4. Training naive scale: (|100 − 80| + |120 − 100| + |140 − 120|)/3 = 20.
5. MASE: 12.5/20 = 0.625.

slides.title: Scaled Forecast Errors
slides.text:
Scaled Forecast Errors

   M22 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 MAPE averages each day’s percentage miss. WAPE compares total absolute error with total
 volume. MASE says the test error is 62.5% of the training naive-error scale; it does not, by
 itself, establish superiority to a naive forecast on the test period. MAPE is undefined at zero
 actuals.
 Why these steps matter
 The denominators intentionally differ. MAPE gives each day’s proportional miss equal weight;
 WAPE evaluates error relative to total volume; MASE compares against a historical forecasting
 scale. A name containing “percentage” is not permission to ignore zeros, signs, or the
 evaluation window.

slides.title: Prediction Intervals
slides.text:
Prediction Intervals

   M24 | Class problem | 8 minutes — Covered, but Useful?

 Treasury receives these purported 90% prediction intervals, in $ millions.
   Day                                            Lower bound   Upper bound          Actual outflow
   1                                                       90                 120              110
   2                                                      100                 120              125
   3                                                       85                 105               95
   4                                                      130                 160              150
   5                                                      100                 110              105
 Count an actual on either boundary as covered. Calculate observed coverage and average width.
 Then lower every lower bound by 10 and raise every upper bound by 10. Recalculate both
 measures. Which result is more useful for treasury?
paragraphs: Prediction Intervals
M24 | Class problem | 8 minutes — Covered, but Useful?

Treasury receives these purported 90% prediction intervals, in $ millions. Day Lower bound Upper bound Actual outflow 1 90 120 110 2 100 120 125 3 85 105 95 4 130 160 150 5 100 110 105 Count an actual on either boundary as covered. Calculate observed coverage and average width. Then lower every lower bound by 10 and raise every upper bound by 10. Recalculate both measures. Which result is more useful for treasury?

slides.title: Prediction Intervals
slides.text:
Prediction Intervals

   M24 | Worked solution — Covered, but Useful?

1. Original coverage: days 1, 3, 4, and 5 are inside; day 2 is outside. Coverage = 4/5 = 80%.
2. Original widths: 30, 20, 20, 30, 10. Mean = 110/5 = $22 million.
3. Widened intervals: [80, 130], [90, 130], [75, 115], [120, 170], [90, 120].
4. Widened coverage: all five actuals are inside, so 5/5 = 100%.
5. Widened average width: each interval grows by 20; 22 + 20 = $42 million.
paragraphs: Prediction Intervals
M24 | Worked solution — Covered, but Useful?

1. Original coverage: days 1, 3, 4, and 5 are inside; day 2 is outside. Coverage = 4/5 = 80%. 2. Original widths: 30, 20, 20, 30, 10. Mean = 110/5 = $22 million. 3. Widened intervals: [80, 130], [90, 130], [75, 115], [120, 170], [90, 120]. 4. Widened coverage: all five actuals are inside, so 5/5 = 100%. 5. Widened average width: each interval grows by 20; 22 + 20 = $42 million.

slides.title: Prediction Intervals
slides.text:
Prediction Intervals

   M24 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Wider ranges cover more outcomes but give less precise funding guidance. Neither result alone
 determines the better system: treasury needs sufficiently reliable coverage and useful width.
 Five observations are too few to conclude that the original 90% intervals are systematically
 miscalibrated.
 Why these steps matter
 Making every interval very wide can raise coverage without giving treasury a useful forecast.
 Coverage and width must be read together, and the five-day count alone is too small to
 establish long-run calibration.

slides.title: Pinball loss – is the quantile forecast wrong in the expensive direction?
slides.text:
Pinball loss – is the quantile forecast wrong in the expensive direction?


 Financial interpretation
 Quantile or pinball loss is useful when underforecasting and overforecasting have different costs, such as
 liquidity buffers or loss reserves.

 Working example: 95th-percentile liquidity need
 The model forecasts the 95th percentile at $130 million.
▶ Actual = $150 million: underforecast by 20; loss = 0.95 × 20 = 19.
▶ Actual = $120 million: overforecast by 10; loss = 0.05 × 10 = 0.5.
 The measure strongly penalizes the dangerous shortage while lightly penalizing excess buffer.

 What it misses
 The chosen quantile must reflect the real risk appetite and cost asymmetry. Validate coverage after
 deployment.

slides.text:
Pinball Loss

   M25 | Formula explained (1/1)

 Question: How should an error be scored when the forecast is intended to be a high quantile?
                                         (
                                          τ (y − q̂),       y ≥ q̂,
                            Lτ (y, q̂) =
                                          (1 − τ )(q̂ − y), y < q̂.
 Read it aloud: If actual demand is above the quantile forecast, multiply the shortage by tau.
 Otherwise multiply the excess by one minus tau.
 Average the daily losses for an overall score. The two branches meet at zero when actual equals
 forecast.
 At tau 0.95, equal-sized under- and overforecasts receive weights 0.95 and 0.05.

slides.title: Pinball Loss
slides.text:
Pinball Loss

   M25 | Worked solution — Penalize a Cash Shortage More Heavily

1. Actual 150: forecast is short by 150 − 130 = 20; loss = 0.95(20) = 19.
2. Actual 120: forecast is high by 130 − 120 = 10; loss = 0.05(10) = 0.5.
3. Actual 130: no error; loss = 0.
4. Average: (19 + 0.5 + 0)/3 = 6.5, in weighted $ million error units.
5. Equal-sized misses: a 10-unit shortage costs 0.95(10) = 9.5 score units; a 10-unit excess
   costs 0.05(10) = 0.5. Ratio = 9.5/0.5 = 19.

slides.title: Pinball Loss
slides.text:
Pinball Loss

   M25 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 This scoring rule strongly discourages underestimating a high liquidity quantile. The 19-to-1
 weighting comes from choosing the 95th percentile; it is not automatically the bank’s actual
 funding-cost ratio. The computed score is not a realized cash loss.
 Why these steps matter
 The high quantile intentionally penalizes shortfalls more than excess. The weights describe the
 scoring target, not observed borrowing fees or a stated regulatory reserve requirement. The
 average 6.5 is in weighted million-dollar error units, not realized loss.

   M26 | Interpretation

 What the answer means

 whether a segmentation is useful.

measures.title: Inertia and Stability
measures.question: act
measures.financialInterpretation: Inertia measures compactness; stability measures whether similar clusters reappear when the data or seed changes.
measures.workingExample: Clusters k 3 4 5 The large improvement from 3 to 4 and smaller improvement from 4 to Inertia 1,200 800 700 5 suggests an elbow near 4. Across bootstrap samples, adjusted Rand index of 0.92 indicates very similar assignments; 0.35 would indicate instability.
measures.whatItMisses: Inertia always falls as k increases. Do not pick the largest k merely because the number is lower.

slides.title: Inertia
slides.text:
Inertia

   M27a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Two groups explain most of the variation here: lower and higher savings. A third adds little
 compactness. Inertia uses squared feature units, not dollars of business value; it also cannot
 establish stability or usefulness. Giving every customer a separate cluster would produce zero
 inertia but no meaningful segmentation.
 Why these steps matter
 The squared distances quantify compactness on the chosen scale. Dividing a group into smaller
 groups can reduce the total even if no useful business distinction is added, so the minimum
 inertia alone is not a defensible stopping rule.

slides.title: Adjusted Rand Index
slides.text:
Adjusted Rand Index

   M27b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 These two runs disagree substantially on who belongs together; agreement is below the
 chance-adjusted reference for these cluster sizes. The value is not “negative accuracy.” Cluster
 names are arbitrary: exchanging X and Y would leave ARI unchanged. This small exercise does
 not establish stability for the bank’s full customer population.
 Why these steps matter
 Compute pair counts, not percentages of matching letters. A relabeling can change every
 displayed group name without moving any customer. ARI therefore ignores names and compares
 the underlying grouping structure.

 pooling all retrieved chunks into one global numerator and denominator.

slides.title: nDCG
slides.text:
nDCG

   M29b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The retriever found the strongest passage but put it behind weaker evidence. Its discounted
 relevance score is about 71% of the ideal ordering’s score. Moving the grade-3 passage first
 gives nDCG of 1 here. Neither score establishes that the generated answer uses the passage
 correctly.
 Why these steps matter
 The normalized result is a fraction of ideal discounted relevance, not the fraction of sources
 that are relevant. Ranking the strongest source second loses more credit under exponential gain
 than a simple relevant-versus-irrelevant count would reveal.

 A true statement can carry the wrong citation, and a well-cited answer can still contain false

 counting rubric is part of the definition, not a formatting detail.

slides.title: Sharpe and Sortino
slides.text:
Sharpe and Sortino

   M31 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 B’s higher return came with more risk. It does not win on either risk-adjusted ratio here. A
 Sharpe ratio of 0.50 means half a unit of excess return per unit of measured volatility—not a
 50% return or a 50% chance of profit. These estimates do not establish future performance or
 tail safety.
 Why these steps matter
 The numerator rewards performance above the specified reference. The denominator identifies
 the kind of variability being charged against that performance. B’s extra return is not enough to
 overcome its larger total volatility on Sharpe, while both funds have the same return per unit of
 supplied downside deviation.

slides.text:
Maximum drawdown, turnover, and tracking error – can the strategy
 survive and be implemented?


 Financial interpretation
 These measures capture investor pain, trading cost, and deviation from a benchmark – dimensions that
 average return does not show.

 Working example
▶ Portfolio rises from 100 to 120, then falls to 90: max drawdown = (120 − 90)/120 = 25%.
▶ Weights move from [50, 30, 20]% to [30, 50, 20]%: one-way turnover = 12 (20 + 20 + 0) = 20%.
▶ If active returns have 3% standard deviation, tracking error is 3%.

 What it misses
 Report transaction cost, liquidity, taxes, and hard constraint violations. An optimizer is unacceptable if any
 mandatory constraint is breached.

slides.title: Maximum Drawdown
slides.text:
Maximum Drawdown

   M32a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 An investor ended up 25% but first endured a one-third decline from the account’s earlier peak.
 Final return hides that path. The later value of 125 cannot be used as the peak for the earlier
 decline to 80.
 Why these steps matter
 The denominator is the earlier peak of 120, not the starting value of 100 or the later value of
 125. The numerator measures the investor’s decline from that peak. A strong final return
 cannot remove the funding or behavioral strain experienced during the earlier drawdown.

   M32b | Worked solution — Can the Allocation Be Implemented?

1. Weight changes: [−20, +10, +10] percentage points.
2. One-way turnover: (20 + 10 + 10)/2 = 20%, equivalent to $200,000 on one side.
3. Trades: sell $200,000 of A; buy $100,000 of B and $100,000 of C. Gross traded value
   = $400, 000.

   turnover.

   50% cap by 5 percentage points, or $50,000.

Tracking Error

   M32c | Interpretation

 What the answer means

 underperformance. Mean monthly active return is zero here, yet active risk is positive.

 data.

 measures that fluctuation. Computing the standard deviation of the fund’s returns alone would
 answer a different question about total risk rather than benchmark-relative risk.

Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall – how large can tail loss become?


 Financial interpretation
 VaR gives a loss threshold at a confidence level. Expected Shortfall gives the average loss beyond that
 threshold and is more informative about the tail.

 Working example
 In 10,000 one-day loss scenarios, 99% VaR is $2.0 million. About 100 scenarios are worse than $2.0 million.
 Their average loss is $3.4 million, so 99% Expected Shortfall is $3.4 million. Interpretation: Under the
 model, only 1% of days are expected to lose more than $2.0 million; when that happens, the average
 modeled loss is $3.4 million.

 What it misses
 VaR is not the maximum loss. Both measures depend on distribution, correlation, liquidity, and regime
 assumptions.

   M33 | Class problem | 8 minutes — Threshold versus Tail Average

 A risk model produces these 10 equally weighted one-day loss scenarios, in $ thousands:
                                                  [10, 0, 5, 20, 1, 7, 3, 6, 2, 4].
 Use 80% confidence to keep the hand calculation small.
▶ VaR: sort losses and choose observation ⌈0.80N ⌉ using the nearest-rank convention.
▶ Expected Shortfall: average the losses in the worst 20% of scenarios.

 largest possible loss? State the horizon with your answer.

A risk model produces these 10 equally weighted one-day loss scenarios, in $ thousands: [10, 0, 5, 20, 1, 7, 3, 6, 2, 4]. Use 80% confidence to keep the hand calculation small. ▶ VaR: sort losses and choose observation ⌈0.80N ⌉ using the nearest-rank convention. ▶ Expected Shortfall: average the losses in the worst 20% of scenarios. Calculate VaR, Expected Shortfall, and the observed fraction strictly exceeding VaR. Is VaR the largest possible loss? State the horizon with your answer.

slides.title: VaR and Expected Shortfall
slides.text:
VaR and Expected Shortfall

   M33 | Worked solution — Threshold versus Tail Average

1. Sort losses: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 20].
2. Locate VaR: ⌈0.80 × 10⌉ = 8. The eighth loss is 7.
                                 V aR80%,1 day = $7, 000.
3. Identify the tail: worst 20% × 10 = 2 scenarios have losses 10 and 20.
                             ES80%,1 day = (10 + 20)/2 = $15, 000.
4. Strict exceedances: 10 and 20 exceed 7, so 2/10 = 20%.
paragraphs: VaR and Expected Shortfall
M33 | Worked solution — Threshold versus Tail Average

1. Sort losses: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 20]. 2. Locate VaR: ⌈0.80 × 10⌉ = 8. The eighth loss is 7. V aR80%,1 day = $7, 000. 3. Identify the tail: worst 20% × 10 = 2 scenarios have losses 10 and 20. ES80%,1 day = (10 + 20)/2 = $15, 000. 4. Strict exceedances: 10 and 20 exceed 7, so 2/10 = 20%.

slides.title: VaR and Expected Shortfall
slides.text:
VaR and Expected Shortfall

   M33 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Under this empirical scenario distribution, 80% of one-day losses are no more than $7,000; the
 worst fifth averages $15,000. VaR is not a maximum loss: even this tiny sample includes a
 $20,000 loss. The 80% level is a teaching choice, not a recommended risk policy.
 Why these steps matter
 VaR identifies where the tail begins under the chosen convention. Expected Shortfall describes
 the size of losses within that tail. They can differ considerably because the threshold does not
 reveal how far the worst observations extend beyond it. Both are conditional on the supplied
 scenario distribution.

 about whether the financial assumptions are correct.

VaR Exceptions

   M35 | Class problem | 7 minutes — Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?

 A bank evaluates a 99% one-day VaR forecast over 250 trading days. Actual daily losses
 exceed that day’s predicted VaR on 10 days. Six of those exceptions occur within one 10-day
 period.
 Calculate:
1. The observed exception rate.
2. The nominal expected number of exceptions under the 99% target.
3. The ratio of observed to nominal exception rates.
 Explain why reviewing only the annual exception count would miss something important. Does
 the count alone identify the cause of the problem?
paragraphs: VaR Exceptions
M35 | Class problem | 7 minutes — Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?

A bank evaluates a 99% one-day VaR forecast over 250 trading days. Actual daily losses exceed that day’s predicted VaR on 10 days. Six of those exceptions occur within one 10-day period. Calculate: 1. The observed exception rate. 2. The nominal expected number of exceptions under the 99% target. 3. The ratio of observed to nominal exception rates. Explain why reviewing only the annual exception count would miss something important. Does the count alone identify the cause of the problem?

slides.title: VaR Exceptions
slides.text:
VaR Exceptions

   M35 | Worked solution — Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?

1. Observed exception rate: 10/250 = 4%.
2. Nominal exception probability: 1 − 0.99 = 1%.
3. Expected count: 250(0.01) = 2.5 exceptions—not a guaranteed count or an acceptance
   band.
4. Rate ratio: 4%/1% = 4× the nominal rate.
5. Timing: six exceptions concentrated in ten days can reveal a stress-period weakness hidden
   by an annual average.
paragraphs: VaR Exceptions
M35 | Worked solution — Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?

1. Observed exception rate: 10/250 = 4%. 2. Nominal exception probability: 1 − 0.99 = 1%. 3. Expected count: 250(0.01) = 2.5 exceptions—not a guaranteed count or an acceptance band. 4. Rate ratio: 4%/1% = 4× the nominal rate. 5. Timing: six exceptions concentrated in ten days can reveal a stress-period weakness hidden by an annual average.

slides.title: VaR Exceptions
slides.text:
VaR Exceptions

   M35 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The model’s tail forecast deserves investigation: exceptions are more frequent than its nominal
 target, and many are clustered. Frequency tests, dependence checks, breach sizes, and market
 or data changes are needed to assess the problem. The count alone does not prove a particular
 cause or quantify losses beyond VaR.
 Why these steps matter
 Using the daily matching forecast matters: comparing every day against one convenient
 annual-average VaR would change the test. The nominal 1% rate follows from the 99% target;
 it does not explain why this sample’s observed rate is 4% or why six exceptions appeared close
 together.

 Reward equals negative cost, and rewards are undiscounted for this exercise. A TWAP
 baseline costs $1,200. The best feasible schedule chosen with hindsight costs $700.
 Calculate cumulative reward, dollar improvement over TWAP, and hindsight regret. Express the
 last two values in basis points of order value. One basis point is 0.0001 of the notional.

A desk executes a $1 million order over three intervals. All compared schedules complete the order. Costs include the same execution-cost components. Interval Learned policy cost 1 $300 2 $200 3 $400 Reward equals negative cost, and rewards are undiscounted for this exercise. A TWAP baseline costs $1,200. The best feasible schedule chosen with hindsight costs $700. Calculate cumulative reward, dollar improvement over TWAP, and hindsight regret. Express the last two values in basis points of order value. One basis point is 0.0001 of the notional.

slides.title: Reward and Regret
slides.text:
Reward and Regret

   M36 | Worked solution — Better Than the Baseline, Short of Hindsight

1. Policy total cost: 300 + 200 + 400 = $900.
2. Cumulative reward: −300 − 200 − 400 = −$900 in the chosen reward units.
3. Improvement over TWAP: 1,200 − 900 = $300.
4. Hindsight regret: 900 − 700 = $200.
5. One basis point of this order: 1,000,000 × 0.0001 = $100. Improvement
   = 300/100 = 3 bps; regret = 200/100 = 2 bps.

M36 | Worked solution — Better Than the Baseline, Short of Hindsight

1. Policy total cost: 300 + 200 + 400 = $900. 2. Cumulative reward: −300 − 200 − 400 = −$900 in the chosen reward units. 3. Improvement over TWAP: 1,200 − 900 = $300. 4. Hindsight regret: 900 − 700 = $200. 5. One basis point of this order: 1,000,000 × 0.0001 = $100. Improvement = 300/100 = 3 bps; regret = 200/100 = 2 bps.

slides.title: Reward and Regret
slides.text:
Reward and Regret

   M36 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The policy saves 3 basis points versus TWAP but costs 2 basis points more than the hindsight
 schedule. Hindsight has information the live policy did not possess. A less negative reward is
 better here; reward becomes economically misleading if material costs or incomplete-order
 penalties are omitted.
 Why these steps matter
 The policy can beat a realistic baseline while still falling short of hindsight. Those are different
 comparisons and should not be combined. The order-value denominator turns dollar differences
 into comparable cost fractions, while the reward sign convention determines which numerical
 direction is better.

Latency

   M39a | Class problem | 9 minutes — The Average Can Pass While the Service Fails

 A fraud-scoring service handles 100 requests, with eventual response times:
   Requests                                            Latency each
   95                                                  40 ms
   4                                                   180 ms
   1                                                   1,000 ms

 Calculate mean latency, p95, and p99. Use the nearest-rank percentile: rank ⌈pN ⌉ in ascending
 order.
 The caller treats any response after 100 ms as a deadline failure, even if a result later arrives.
 Calculate this timeout/deadline-failure rate. The service objective requires 99% of requests
 within 100 ms. Does this sample meet it?

A fraud-scoring service handles 100 requests, with eventual response times: Requests Latency each 95 40 ms 4 180 ms 1 1,000 ms

Calculate mean latency, p95, and p99. Use the nearest-rank percentile: rank ⌈pN ⌉ in ascending order. The caller treats any response after 100 ms as a deadline failure, even if a result later arrives. Calculate this timeout/deadline-failure rate. The service objective requires 99% of requests within 100 ms. Does this sample meet it?

slides.title: Latency
slides.text:
Latency

   M39a | Worked solution — The Average Can Pass While the Service Fails

1. Total latency: 95(40) + 4(180) + 1(1,000) = 3,800 + 720 + 1,000 = 5,520 ms.
2. Mean: 5,520/100 = 55.2 ms.
3. p95: rank ⌈0.95(100)⌉ = 95; latency = 40 ms.
4. p99: rank 99 lies among the four 180 ms requests; p99 = 180 ms.
5. Deadline failures: 4 + 1 = 5 requests; 5/100 = 5%. Only 95% finish within 100 ms.

   M39a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The mean and p95 look fast, but the 99%-within-100-ms objective is missed. Five payment
 decisions arrive too late for the caller. The percentile convention and treatment of late
 responses are stated explicitly so the result can be reproduced.
 Why these steps matter
 The 95 fast requests dominate the average and determine p95. The next four requests
 determine p99 and create deadline failures along with the slowest request. Averaging the three
 latency values without their request counts would give each group the wrong weight.

   M39b | Class problem | 9 minutes — Calculate Both Bottlenecks

 A load test establishes a service’s maximum sustained capacity at 12,000 requests per
 minute. New requests arrive at 250 per second for ten minutes. Start with an empty queue;
 assume no dropped requests or extra capacity.
 Separately, the model generates 500 investigation alerts per day. There are 15 analysts,
 each able to finish 20 cases per day. Start with no alert backlog.
 Calculate API capacity per second and the ten-minute request backlog. Then calculate daily
 human capacity, the three-day alert backlog, and required cases per analyst per day to keep up.
paragraphs: Throughput and Review Load

Start with an empty queue; assume no dropped requests or extra capacity. Separately, the model generates 500 investigation alerts per day. There are 15 analysts, each able to finish 20 cases per day. Then calculate daily human capacity, the three-day alert backlog, and required cases per analyst per day to keep up.

slides.title: Throughput and Review Load
slides.text:
Throughput and Review Load

   M39b | Worked solution — Calculate Both Bottlenecks

1. API capacity: 12,000/60 = 200 requests/second.
2. API backlog growth: 250 − 200 = 50 requests/second.
3. Ten-minute backlog: 50 × 10 × 60 = 30, 000 requests.
4. Daily human capacity: 15 × 20 = 300 cases.
5. Daily unworked alerts: 500 − 300 = 200. After three days: 200(3) = 600 alerts.
6. Required analyst pace: 500/15 = 33.33 cases/day, versus the available 20.

slides.title: Cost and Abstention
slides.text:
Cost and Abstention

   M39c | Worked solution — Price the Entire Workflow

1. Abstention rate: 100/1,000 = 10%. Automated-answer coverage = 900/1,000 = 90%.
2. Human review cost: 100($3) = $300.
3. Total operating cost: $500 + $300 = $800.
4. Cost per incoming request: 800/1,000 = $0.80.
5. Correctly resolved requests: 800 + 100 = 900.
                      All-in cost per correct resolution = 800/900 ≈ $0.89.
6. Automatic-answer accuracy: 800/900 = 88.89%.

slides.title: Cost and Abstention
slides.text:
Cost and Abstention

   M39c | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Abstention adds review expense and routes those cases to correct manual resolution under the
 exercise’s assumptions. Model spend alone understates operating cost. Even the all-in $0.80 per
 request excludes the consequences of the 100 wrong answers; it is not a complete economic loss
 measure.
 Why these steps matter
 The same numerical fraction can represent different concepts: 800/900 is automatic-answer
 accuracy, while $800 divided by 900 correct resolutions is a cost in dollars. The numerator’s
 units and the denominator’s population determine the meaning. The scenario does not establish
 what automatic answers would have been produced on the abstained cases.

slides.title: Uptime
slides.text:
Uptime

   M39d | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 “Over 99% available” is not enough for the specified 99.9% objective. The service was
 unavailable for more than twice its allotted downtime. Time-based availability also does not
 reveal how many payment requests were affected or whether the outage coincided with peak
 demand.
 Why these steps matter
 A target of 99.9% leaves 0.1% of scheduled time for unavailability, not 0.9%. Multiplying that
 small fraction by the full month’s minutes makes the allowance concrete. The same outage
 length can affect very different payment volumes depending on when it occurs.

slides.title: Working code: calculate core classification measures
slides.text:
Working code: calculate core classification measures


  import numpy as np
  from sklearn.metrics import (
      confusion_matrix, precision_score, recall_score,
      f1_score, roc_auc_score, average_precision_score,
      brier_score_loss, log_loss
  )

  y_true = np.array([0,0,1,0,1,0,0,1,0,1])
  y_score = np.array([.05,.20,.90,.30,.70,.40,.10,.60,.80,.55])
  y_pred = (y_score >= .50).astype(int)

  print("confusion matrix\n", confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred))
  print("precision", precision_score(y_true, y_pred))
  print("recall", recall_score(y_true, y_pred))
  print("F1", f1_score(y_true, y_pred))
  print("ROC-AUC", roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score))
  print("PR-AUC", average_precision_score(y_true, y_score))
  print("Brier", brier_score_loss(y_true, y_score))
  print("log loss", log_loss(y_true, y_score))

 Change the threshold from 0.50 to 0.70. Which measures move, which do not, and which operating decision
 changes?

slides.title: Working code: calculate forecast and ranking measures
slides.text:
Working code: calculate forecast and ranking measures



  import numpy as np
  from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

  actual   = np.array([100, 120, 80, 150], dtype=float)
  forecast = np.array([ 90, 130,100, 140], dtype=float)

  mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, forecast)
  rmse = mean_squared_error(actual, forecast) ** 0.5
  mape = np.mean(np.abs((actual - forecast) / actual))
  wape = np.abs(actual - forecast).sum() / np.abs(actual).sum()
  r2   = r2_score(actual, forecast)
  print(mae, rmse, mape, wape, r2)

  # Precision@K for a ranked fraud queue
  labels = np.array([1,0,1,1,0,0,1,0,0,0])
  k = 5
  print("precision@k", labels[:k].mean())
  print("recall@k", labels[:k].sum() / labels.sum())

A training node contains 10 transactions: 4 frauds and 6 legitimate transactions. A

solutionPages.title: Trees and Random Forests
solutionPages.text:
Trees and Random Forests

   A02 | Worked solution — A Fraud Split

1. Parent impurity: 1 − 0.42 − 0.62 = 0.48.
2. Child impurities:
                                               Gnew = 1 − (3/4)2 − (1/4)2 = 0.375.
                                             Gtrusted = 1 − (1/6)2 − (5/6)2 = 0.2778.
3. Weight the children:
                      Gsplit = (4/10)(0.375) + (6/10)(0.2778) = 0.3167.
                                            Impurity reduction = 0.48 − 0.3167 = 0.1633.
4. Average the tree outputs: (0.75 + 0.50 + 0.25)/3 = 0.50.
5. Apply the threshold: The forest does not trigger a challenge because 0.50 < 0.60. The first
   tree alone would trigger one because 0.75 ≥ 0.60.

interpretationPages.title: Trees and Random Forests
interpretationPages.text:
Trees and Random Forests

   A02 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The split creates more uniform groups in this training sample. Averaging trees changes the
 intervention decision; it does not prove that the resulting score is calibrated. Gini impurity
 here is different from the AUC-derived Gini coefficient.
 Why these steps matter
 Child size matters: averaging the two child impurities 50/50 would incorrectly give the
 four-record group as much influence as the six-record group. The forest score and the split
 impurity answer different questions; neither is a measured probability calibration result.

 increment produces different probability changes at different starting scores.

readAloud: New score = previous score + learning rate × this tree’s correction. Convert the final score to a probability only after adding the corrections. The tree outputs here are already fitted and supplied. Changing the learning rate scales these fixed contributions for the hand calculation; a newly trained model may learn different trees. Review if the resulting probability reaches 18%, or 0.18.
workedExplanation: Smaller corrections leave the applicant below the review cutoff in this example. The corrections are log-odds increments, not probability percentage points. In a full retraining, changing the learning rate can also change the later fitted trees.

The learning rate changes the amount of correction, not the definition of probability. Adding 0.4 to a log-odds score is not adding 40 percentage points to default risk. The same score increment produces different probability changes at different starting scores.
workedArithmetic: p = 1 / (1 + exp(1.4)) ≈ 0.1978 = 19.78%, which exceeds the 18% review threshold.
p = 1 / (1 + exp(1.7)) ≈ 0.1545 = 15.45%, below the same threshold.

exercises.title: Group Savings Behavior
exercises.question:
A bank groups customers using one feature: the percentage of monthly income saved.
 Four customers save 10%, 20%, 60%, and 70%. Start K-means with two centers: 10% and
 60%.
 Use absolute distance for assignment; with one feature, it produces the same nearest-center
 assignment as squared distance.
1. Assign each customer to the nearest starting center.
2. Update each center to the average of its assigned customers.
3. Assign a new customer who saves 35% using the updated centers.
4. Describe the two groups without claiming that one is more creditworthy.

solutionPages.text:
K-Means

   A04 | Worked solution — Group Savings Behavior

1. Assign customers using the original centers.
   Savings rate                             Distance to 10%   Distance to 60% Assignment
   10%                                                    0                       50 Group 1
   20%                                                   10                       40 Group 1
   60%                                                   50                            0 Group 2
   70%                                                   60                       10 Group 2

2. Update the centers: µ1 = (10 + 20)/2 = 15%; µ2 = (60 + 70)/2 = 65%.
3. Assign the new customer: Distances from 35% are |35 − 15| = 20 and |35 − 65| = 30
   percentage points. Assign the customer to Group 1.

interpretationPages.title: K-Means
interpretationPages.text:
K-Means

   A04 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The groups represent lower and higher observed savings rates. A 15% center is a group average,
 not a required savings target or a default probability. The groups alone do not justify credit
 decisions.
 Why these steps matter
 A cluster center describes the customers currently assigned to it. It is not a rule about how
 much customers should save. This exercise groups one behavior; creditworthiness would require
 a different target and supporting evidence.

   A05 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 A was isolated fastest and receives the highest anomaly score. 0.7071 is not a 70.71% fraud

 Why these steps matter
 Normalization makes the path length a comparable score. It does not add fraud labels. The
 investor or merchant’s intent is absent from this calculation; the available reviewer gets the
 most unusual case, not a mathematically proven fraud.

exercises.title: Forecast Settlement Outflows
exercises.question:
Daily settlement outflows, in $ millions, were 100, 110, and 116 over the last three days.
 A fitted ARIMA(1,1,0) model forecasts changes using:
                                            ∆yt = yt − yt−1 ,   ∆y
                                                                c
                                                                   t+1 = 0.5∆yt .

 Forecast future errors as zero; there is no additional drift term.
1. Forecast the next two daily outflow levels, without using future observations.
2. Treasury adds a fixed $10 million buffer to the first forecast. How much liquidity does it
   hold?
3. The next day’s actual outflow later becomes 125. Compare the model’s absolute error with a
   last-value forecast of 116.

   A06 | Worked solution — Forecast Settlement Outflows

1. Calculate the latest observed change: 116 − 110 = 6 million.
2. Forecast the next change and level:

3. Forecast one more step, using the forecasted change:

4. Add the buffer: 119 + 10 = $129 million.

   error = |125 − 116| = 9 million.

interpretationPages.title: ARIMA
interpretationPages.text:
ARIMA

   A06 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The model reduces this day’s absolute error by $3 million. Treasury’s $129 million holding
 exceeds the realized outflow by $4 million. One successful day does not validate the model or
 establish that the fixed buffer is adequate.
 Why these steps matter
 A forecasted change and a forecasted level have different jobs even though both use dollar units.
 Treasury needs the level to fund settlements. The calculation must not use the actual 125 until
 the evaluation step, because it was unknown when the forecast was issued.

exercises.title: Trace Shared Connections
exercises.question:
At the decision cutoff, an undirected graph contains these links:
    Account A –- Device 7
    Account B –- Device 7
    Account B –- Merchant 9
    Account C –- Merchant 9
    Account D –- Device 8

 A connected component is a set of nodes reachable from one another. A node’s degree is its
 number of direct links.
1. List the connected components and their sizes, counting all node types.
2. Calculate each account’s degree. Which account has the most direct links?
3. Find the shortest path from Account A to Account C; count its edges.
4. Does being in the same component establish that A and C committed fraud?

Graph Methods

   A07 | Worked solution — Trace Shared Connections

1. Follow the links to identify components.
       • Component 1: A, B, C, Device 7, Merchant 9 — 5 nodes.
       • Component 2: D, Device 8 — 2 nodes.
2. Count account links: A has 1; B has 2; C has 1; D has 1. B has the highest account
   degree.
3. Trace the shortest A-to-C route:
                          A → Device 7 → B → M erchant 9 → C.
      The route contains 4 edges.
4. Separate a link from a conclusion: Shared use of a device or merchant may warrant
   investigation, but it is not proof of fraud.

interpretationPages.title: Graph Methods
interpretationPages.text:
Graph Methods

   A07 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 B connects two parts of the account network and may be useful to investigate. Component size
 and degree are relational features, not probabilities or findings of misconduct.
 Why these steps matter
 A four-edge path does not imply four transfers or four criminal steps. Its meaning comes from
 the edge definitions. Device sharing and merchant sharing may produce legitimate links, so
 graph features support investigation rather than establish misconduct.

exercises.question:
A filing parser is audited before the financial Q&A system is evaluated:
▶ Eight tables are checked; seven retain every required header, row, and unit label.
▶ Ten required sections are checked; nine appear in the parsed output.

 For this exercise define table integrity rate as intact tables / audited tables, section coverage
 as present required sections / required sections, and numeric extraction error rate as incorrect
 cells / audited cells.
 Calculate all three. Can high section coverage compensate for a wrongly parsed debt figure?

interpretationPages.title: Parsing Quality
interpretationPages.text:
Parsing Quality

   S01 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The retriever cannot reliably recover information that parsing omitted or corrupted. A filing can
 have most sections present and still support a materially wrong answer. These are separate
 audit measures with explicit classroom definitions, not an invitation to average table, section,
 and cell percentages into one score.
 Why these steps matter
 An intact table is a whole-table success, whereas a numeric error is counted cell by cell. A single
 table can therefore contain multiple erroneous cells, and the three scores need not move
 together. Their averages cannot establish whether a critical debt or covenant value is usable.

solutionPages.title: Answer Exactness and Completeness
solutionPages.text:
Answer Exactness and Completeness

   S02 | Worked solution — Did It Answer the Whole Question?

1. Entirely correct answers: Q1 supplies 2/2 and Q4 supplies 4/4. Q2 and Q3 are incomplete.
2. Answer exactness: 2/4 = 50%.
3. Total required components: 2 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 10.
4. Correctly supplied components: 2 + 2 + 0 + 4 = 8.
5. Component completeness: 8/10 = 80%.

interpretationPages.title: Answer Exactness and Completeness
interpretationPages.text:
Answer Exactness and Completeness

   S02 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The system supplied most required facts but fully answered only half the questions. Reporting
 80% alone would hide the incomplete answers. Components are equally weighted in this
 exercise; missing a critical covenant or denominator may matter more than missing a minor
 descriptive detail.
 Why these steps matter
 Exactness gives every question one vote. Pooled completeness gives every required component
 one vote. A partly answered three-component question can contribute two correct components
 but zero fully correct questions. Neither measure alone establishes whether a missing
 component is financially critical.

A partly answered three-component question can contribute two correct components but zero fully correct questions. Neither measure alone establishes whether a missing component is financially critical.

exercises.title: Choose a Feasible Portfolio
exercises.question:
A hypothetical $100,000 portfolio can use stocks and bonds with these annual estimates:
   Asset                                                     Expected return                          Volatility
   Stocks                                                                 10%                              20%
   Bonds                                                                   4%                               5%

 Assume zero correlation. Policy permits only three stock/bond allocations: 40/60, 50/50,
 and 60/40. Expected return must be at least 7%.
 For stock weight w:
                                µp = 0.10w + 0.04(1 − w),   σp2 = w2 (0.20)2 + (1 − w)2 (0.05)2 .
 Calculate return and volatility for each allocation. Choose the lowest-variance feasible
 candidate, then calculate its dollar allocations.

Constrained Optimization

   A10 | Worked solution — Choose a Feasible Portfolio

1. Calculate return and variance for each allowed candidate.
   Stock weight                             Expected return Variance calculation                Volatility Feasible?
   40%                                            0.4(10) +   0.0064 + 0.0009 =                      8.54% No

3. Compare feasible candidates: 50/50 has lower variance than 60/40.
4. Allocate dollars: 100,000(0.50) = $50,000 to each asset.

learning.title: Choose a Feasible Portfolio
learning.scenario: A portfolio may use only the listed stock weights; the remaining weight goes to bonds. Stocks and bonds have zero correlation. Expected return must meet the supplied minimum.
learning.task: Calculate return and volatility for each candidate. Among feasible candidates, choose the lowest variance and calculate dollar allocations.
learning.interpretation: Check feasibility before comparing risk. This is an optimum among the listed candidates under estimated inputs; expected return and volatility are not guarantees.

hints: Take the square root of each candidate variance.

hints: Multiply portfolio value by the chosen stock weight.

bondDollars.title: Dollar allocation to bonds
hints: Multiply portfolio value by one minus the chosen stock weight.

readAloud: Expected return is a weighted average. Variance combines each asset’s weighted risk and a co-movement term. Take its square root for volatility. Here correlation is zero, so the last term is zero. Enter 20% volatility as 0.20 before squaring.

Only the three supplied stock weights are allowed, and expected return must reach 7%. Discard candidates that fail; choose the remaining one with smallest variance. Stock dollars = V w, Bond dollars = V (1 − w). Multiply total portfolio value by each allocation weight to turn fractions into dollars. This is a finite candidate comparison, not a claim that the best choice over every possible investment has been found.
workedExplanation: The lowest-risk candidate overall fails the return constraint. 50/50 is optimal only among these three permitted candidates under the supplied estimates. Neither the 7% expected return nor the volatility is guaranteed.

Compare variance only after checking feasibility. A low-risk allocation can fail a mandatory return requirement. The covariance term is shown so students can see exactly what the zero-correlation assumption removes; the example assumes zero correlation.
workedArithmetic: At 40% stocks: return = 0.4 × 10% + 0.6 × 4% = 6.4%; variance = 0.4² × 0.20² + 0.6² × 0.05² = 0.0073; volatility = √0.0073 ≈ 8.54%. This fails the 7% return minimum.
The 50/50 candidate has the lower feasible variance. Stock and bond allocations are each $100,000 × 0.50 = $50,000.

exercises.title: Update an Execution Decision
exercises.question:
A trading simulator records negative costs as rewards: less negative is better.
 For the action “buy now,” Q(s, a) = −5. The action produces immediate reward r = −2. At
 the next state, the available action values are −4 and −1.
 Use learning rate α = 0.5 and discount factor γ = 0.9:
                                           h                       i
                         Qnew = Qold + α r + γ max Q(s′ , a) − Qold .
                                                         a

 The alternative action “wait” currently has value −4.2.
1. Calculate the update target, update error, and new “buy now” value.
2. Which action does a greedy policy now select?
3. What would the update target be if the transition ended the episode?

formulaPages.title: Q-Learning
formulaPages.text:
Q-Learning

   A11 | Formula explained (1/1)

 Question: How should one observation update the estimated value of “buy now”?
                                            T = r + γ max Q(s′ , a),   δ = T − Qold ,
                                                        a
                                                       Qnew = Qold + αδ.
 Read it aloud: Target = immediate reward + discounted best next-state value. Update error
 = target minus old estimate. Move the old estimate a fraction of the way toward the target.
 These three steps are the original Q-learning update written separately. If the transition ends
 the episode, the future-value term is zero.
 The greedy choice selects the largest current action value. With negative costs as rewards, less
 negative is better.

solutionPages.title: Q-Learning
solutionPages.text:
Q-Learning

   A11 | Worked solution — Update an Execution Decision

1. Choose the best next-state value: max(−4, −1) = −1.
2. Calculate the target: −2 + 0.9(−1) = −2.9.
3. Calculate the update error: −2.9 − (−5) = 2.1.
4. Apply the learning rate:
                                            Qnew = −5 + 0.5(2.1) = −3.95.
5. Compare current actions: Buy now has −3.95 versus waiting at −4.2. A greedy policy
   chooses buy now because −3.95 is higher.
6. Terminal case: No future reward remains, so the target is the immediate reward −2.

interpretationPages.title: Q-Learning
interpretationPages.text:
Q-Learning

   A11 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The observation made “buy now” look less costly than previously estimated. The Q-value
 estimates discounted future reward in the simulator; it is not a guaranteed trading outcome or a
 probability.
 Why these steps matter
 Subtracting an old negative value means adding its magnitude when calculating the update
 error. A positive update error raises the Q-value, meaning this observation makes the action
 look better. Neither the target nor the updated value is a probability.

interpretationPages.title: Implementation Shortfall
interpretationPages.text:
Implementation Shortfall

   S03 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Looking only at executed prices would omit the cost of missing 200 shares while the market
 rose. The opportunity cost is a benchmark-based estimate, not a cash fee. The stated shortfall
 convention and completion rate should accompany the result.
 Why these steps matter
 The intended order is the economic reference. Ignoring unfilled shares could make a policy look
 cheap simply by avoiding trades while the market moves against the unfinished order. Reporting
 completion alongside full-order shortfall exposes that failure.

readAloud: For each fill, multiply shares bought by the extra price above arrival. Add the benchmark cost of shares left unfilled when the price moved, then add fees. This is the buy-order convention specified in the exercise. A higher execution or closing price produces a positive cost. The unfilled-share term is a benchmark opportunity cost, not a paid transaction fee.

Add filled quantities and divide by the intended quantity. Multiply the intended quantity by the arrival price for the original target notional, then express total shortfall as basis points of that amount. Do not change the denominator to the executed portion merely because some shares remain unfilled.
workedExplanation: Looking only at executed prices would omit the cost of missing 200 shares while the market rose. The opportunity cost is a benchmark-based estimate, not a cash fee. The stated shortfall convention and completion rate should accompany the result.

The intended order is the economic reference. Ignoring unfilled shares could make a policy look cheap simply by avoiding trades while the market moves against the unfinished order. Reporting completion alongside full-order shortfall exposes that failure.

solutionPages.title: Tail Slippage
solutionPages.text:
Tail Slippage

   S04 | Worked solution — A Better Average Can Hide Worse Executions

1. Mean: total = 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 20 + 30 = 94; mean = 94/10 = 9.4 bps.
2. p90: rank ⌈0.90(10)⌉ = 9; result = 20 bps.
3. p95: rank ⌈0.95(10)⌉ = 10; result = 30 bps.
4. Worst 20%: two largest costs, 20 and 30; average = 25 bps.
5. Baseline: mean and worst-20% average are both 12 bps.
paragraphs: Tail Slippage
S04 | Worked solution — A Better Average Can Hide Worse Executions

1. Mean: total = 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 20 + 30 = 94; mean = 94/10 = 9.4 bps. 2. p90: rank ⌈0.90(10)⌉ = 9; result = 20 bps. 3. p95: rank ⌈0.95(10)⌉ = 10; result = 30 bps. 4. Worst 20%: two largest costs, 20 and 30; average = 25 bps. 5. Baseline: mean and worst-20% average are both 12 bps.

interpretationPages.title: Tail Slippage
interpretationPages.text:
Tail Slippage

   S04 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The learned policy improves average cost by 2.6 bps, but its worst fifth costs 13 bps more than
 the baseline’s worst fifth. Choosing between them requires an explicit tolerance for execution tail
 risk. Ten orders are enough for arithmetic, not for a reliable estimate of future tail performance.
 Why these steps matter
 The mean can improve when many orders get slightly cheaper even as a few become much more
 expensive. Percentiles describe thresholds and the tail mean describes the average beyond the
 selected worst-fraction boundary. Neither the small sample nor a lower overall mean establishes
 acceptable future tail behavior.

interpretationPages.title: Monte Carlo
interpretationPages.text:
Monte Carlo

   A12 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Five runs produce noisy estimates: $4,000 versus a true model mean of $2,000, and 20%
 versus a true model breach probability of 4%. More independent runs reduce simulation
 noise; they do not validate the assumed 20% default probability or independence.
 Why these steps matter
 The default indicators are 0/1, the portfolio losses are dollars, and the breach estimate is a
 proportion. Analytical expected loss does not require independent defaults when the individual
 expected losses are given; independence is required for the simple product used to calculate the
 probability that both loans default.

workedArithmetic: Loss per default = $10,000 × 0.50 = $5,000. The five default patterns are A only, neither, both, neither, B only, giving losses [$5,000, $0, $10,000, $0, $5,000].
Simulated mean = (5,000 + 0 + 10,000 + 0 + 5,000) / 5 = $4,000. Only the third loss exceeds $5,000, so estimated breach probability = 1/5 = 20%.
Under independence, both-default probability = 0.20 × 0.20 = 4%. Here both defaults are needed to exceed the reserve.

exercises.title: Count the Four Outcomes
exercises.question:
A fraud detector processes 1,000 transactions. Later investigation establishes that 20 were
 fraud.
 The detector flagged 50 transactions. Of the flagged transactions, 15 were fraud.
 Treat fraud as the positive class and a flag as a positive prediction.
1. Fill in all four cells: true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives.
2. Verify that the four counts add to 1,000.
3. How many legitimate customers were interrupted, and how many frauds were missed?
   Decision                                        Actually fraud                    Actually legitimate

solutionPages.text:
Confusion Matrix

   M01 | Worked solution — Count the Four Outcomes

1. True positives: The 15 confirmed frauds among the flags give T P = 15.
2. False positives: F P = 50 − 15 = 35.
3. False negatives: F N = 20 − 15 = 5.
4. True negatives: There are 1,000 − 20 = 980 legitimate transactions, so
   T N = 980 − 35 = 945.
   Decision                                       Actually fraud                   Actually legitimate
   Flagged                                                   15                                    35
   Not flagged                                                 5                                  945
 Check: 15 + 35 + 5 + 945 = 1,000.

interpretationPages.title: Accuracy
interpretationPages.text:
Accuracy

   M02 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 98% accuracy can describe a system that provides no fraud detection. Accuracy counts
 every mistake equally, although a missed fraud and a false alert may have very different costs.
 More information is needed to decide whether the detector’s additional interruptions are
 worthwhile.
 Why these steps matter
 The 96% result refers to all transactions, including the many legitimate cases. The loss of two
 percentage points versus the baseline does not tell you whether catching 15 frauds compensates
 for the 35 false alerts. That requires a cost model.

interpretationPages.title: Balanced Accuracy
interpretationPages.text:
Balanced Accuracy

   M03 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The detector performs substantially better when fraud and legitimate transactions receive equal
 class-level weight: 85.71% versus 50%. This still does not price errors in dollars. Balanced
 accuracy is not a claim that 85.71% of all individual transactions were classified correctly.
 Why these steps matter
 Balanced accuracy first normalizes within each class. The rare fraud class therefore contributes
 as much as the much larger legitimate class. It is still a statistical weighting convention, not a
 financial cost weighting.

solutionPages.title: Precision
solutionPages.text:
Precision

   M04 | Worked solution — How Productive Is the Review Queue?

1. Precision: Queue A = 15/50 = 30%; Queue B = 8/10 = 80%.
2. Total review cost: A = 50(4) = $200; B = 10(4) = $40.
3. Review cost per confirmed fraud:
                        A = 200/15 = $13.33,              B = 40/8 = $5.00.
4. Compare capture: A finds 15 frauds; B finds only 8, despite its higher precision.

interpretationPages.title: Precision
interpretationPages.text:
Precision

   M04 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 B uses investigator time more efficiently: 80% of its alerts are genuine fraud, versus 30%
 for A. But A finds 7 additional frauds. Their loss amounts and the remaining review capacity
 matter before selecting a policy. Precision measures queue quality, not total fraud coverage.
 Why these steps matter
 The numerator of precision is a count of useful discoveries, while the numerator of cost per
 fraud is dollars. Keeping the units visible prevents treating an 80% precision result as an 80%
 reduction in fraud losses.

formulaPages.title: Recall
formulaPages.text:
Recall

   M05 | Formula explained (1/1)

 Question: What fraction of fraud was found, and how much loss remains from misses?
                                       TP
                         Recall =             ,    F N = F − T P,

                                     Lmiss = cF N F N.
 Read it aloud: Divide caught frauds by all actual frauds. Subtract the caught count from the
 total to find misses. Multiply misses by the assumed loss per miss.

 same US$2,000 loss, the capture fractions also describe the share of fraud value detected here.

solutionPages.title: Recall
solutionPages.text:
Recall

   M05 | Worked solution — Put a Price on Missed Fraud

1. Recall: A = 15/20 = 75%; B = 8/20 = 40%.
2. Frauds missed: A = 20 − 15 = 5; B = 20 − 8 = 12.
3. Residual loss:
                                          A = 5(2,000) = $10,000,   B = 12(2,000) = $24,000.
4. Difference: 24,000 − 10,000 = $14,000.
paragraphs: Recall
M05 | Worked solution — Put a Price on Missed Fraud

interpretationPages.title: Recall
interpretationPages.text:
Recall

   M05 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 A captures 75% of fraud events and leaves $14,000 less modeled missed-fraud loss than
 B. This is event recall; it equals value capture here only because fraud losses are assumed equal.
 False alerts, review costs, and intervention effectiveness are still needed for the overall decision.
 Why these steps matter
 A higher recall can reduce the number of missed frauds, but it does not describe the cost of the
 extra flags. The modeled US$14,000 difference is a comparison of missed-fraud loss only, not
 a complete profit comparison.

solutionPages.title: Specificity and FPR
solutionPages.text:
Specificity and FPR

   M06 | Worked solution — Count Customer Interruptions

1. Specificity: 945/980 = 0.964286 = 96.43%.
2. False-positive rate: 35/980 = 0.035714 = 3.57%.
3. Check: 96.43% + 3.57% = 100% after rounding.
4. Scale to production:
                                                  1,000,000(35/980) ≈ 35,714 false alerts.
5. Use the correct denominator: FPR asks what fraction of legitimate activity was
   disturbed. A denominator of all alerts would answer a different question about queue quality.

interpretationPages.title: Specificity and FPR
interpretationPages.text:
Specificity and FPR

   M06 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 A false-positive rate of about 3.57% would create roughly 35,714 interruptions per million
 legitimate transactions, under the unchanged-rate assumption. A small-looking rate can
 create a large operational burden.
 Why these steps matter
 FPR divides false alerts by legitimate transactions. One minus precision instead divides false
 alerts by all alerts. The same numerator can appear in two metrics with very different business
 meanings because their denominators differ.

readAloud: Among legitimate transactions, divide the passed count or the flagged count by the same legitimate total. Multiply the false-positive fraction by future legitimate volume to estimate interruptions. The production-volume calculation assumes the false-positive rate remains unchanged.
workedExplanation: A false-positive rate of about 3.57% would create roughly 35,714 interruptions per million legitimate transactions, under the unchanged-rate assumption. A small-looking rate can create a large operational burden.

FPR divides false alerts by legitimate transactions. One minus precision instead divides false alerts by all alerts. The same numerator can appear in two metrics with very different business meanings because their denominators differ.
