formulaPages.title: F1 and F-beta
formulaPages.text:
F1 and F-beta

   M07 | Formula explained (1/1)

 Question: How can precision and recall be summarized in one score?
                                                          2P R            (1 + β 2 )P R
                                                  F1 =         ,   Fβ =                 .
                                                         P +R              β2P + R
 Read it aloud: F1 is twice the product divided by the sum: the harmonic mean of precision and
 recall. F-beta changes the weighting of that combination.
 For F2, set beta to 2 and beta-squared to 4. This places more emphasis on recall than F1 does.
 It does not encode a particular dollar-cost ratio.
 Compare with the arithmetic mean, (P + R)/2, which is an ordinary equal-weight average.

interpretationPages.title: F1 and F-beta
interpretationPages.text:
F1 and F-beta

   M07 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 F1 = 0.429 summarizes the tradeoff; F2 = 0.577 places more emphasis on the stronger recall.
 These are differently weighted scores, not two competing models. Neither score contains dollar
 loss, investigator capacity, or probability calibration.
 Why these steps matter
 F1 and F2 are two summaries of the same operating point. A larger F2 does not mean the
 detector has improved. It means the selected weighting gives more credit to the detector’s
 relatively high recall.

   0.65                            A, B, C         2               1               33.33%         66.67%

interpretationPages.title: ROC
interpretationPages.text:
ROC

   M08 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Each ROC point represents a different capture-versus-interruption tradeoff. These are selected
 points, not the full curve. The ROC curve itself does not choose the economically appropriate
 threshold.
 Why these steps matter
 The curve shows possible operating choices, not one mandatory threshold. Moving toward
 higher capture may also interrupt more legitimate activity. In this small set, the denominators
 stay fixed, so changes in rates come entirely from changes in the flagged cases.

solutionPages.title: ROC-AUC and Gini
solutionPages.text:
ROC-AUC and Gini

   M09 | Worked solution — Count Correct Rankings

1. Compare every fraud score with every legitimate score.
   Fraud score                           Beats 0.80?   Beats 0.40?   Beats 0.10?                Points
   0.90                                  Yes           Yes           Yes                             3
   0.70                                  No            Yes           Yes                             2
   0.30                                  No            No            Yes                             1

2. Add ranking points: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6; there are no ties.
3. AUC: 6/9 = 0.6667.
4. Gini: 2(0.6667) − 1 = 0.3333.

interpretationPages.text:
ROC-AUC and Gini

   M09 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The model ranks a fraud above a legitimate transaction in two-thirds of these pairs. AUC is
 not threshold-specific accuracy, a fraud probability, or a profit estimate. This Gini is a rescaling
 of ranking AUC, not tree-node impurity.
 Why these steps matter
 AUC uses all nine fraud–legitimate comparisons. Accuracy at a particular cutoff would use six
 yes/no decisions instead. The two fractions summarize different questions even when calculated
 from the same records.

   M10 | Worked solution — Find the Largest Separation

1. Divide each class count by its own total.
   Cutoff                                         Default capture   Non-default capture         Absolute gap

   those evaluated.

interpretationPages.title: KS
interpretationPages.text:
KS

   M10 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 At B, the model has captured 60% of defaults but only 15% of non-defaults. That separation is
 a ranking diagnostic. Choosing a lending action still requires loss severity, approval value,
 capacity, and policy constraints.
 Why these steps matter
 Dividing both counts by all 100 applicants would answer a different question. KS compares
 within-class capture rates, so each class needs its own denominator. The biggest statistical
 gap does not include lending margins or loss severity.

interpretationPages.title: Precision–Recall Curve
interpretationPages.text:
Precision–Recall Curve

   M11a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Reviewing six cases captures every fraud in this sample, but half the queue is legitimate. An
 empirical precision–recall curve can rise locally; precision does not necessarily fall at every
 additional rank.
 Why these steps matter
 Recall cannot decrease when the queue only expands, because caught frauds are not removed.
 Precision can rise or fall: its numerator and denominator change differently depending on
 whether the next case is fraud.

interpretationPages.title: Average Precision and PR-AUC
interpretationPages.text:
Average Precision and PR-AUC

   M11b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 AP = 0.7222 and trapezoidal PR-area = 0.6778 describe the same ranking using different
 interpolation conventions. AP is a recall-weighted summary of precision, not “72.22% of
 transactions are correct.” Report the convention explicitly when comparing models.
 Why these steps matter
 The difference between 0.7222 and 0.6778 is not a change in the model or its ranking. It comes
 from the way the curve’s area is summarized. Comparing these two numbers as if they were the
 same statistic would manufacture a performance difference.

exercises.title: Match Review Capacity
exercises.question:
A batch contains 100 transactions and 8 actual frauds.
 The top 5 model-ranked transactions contain 3 frauds. The top 10 contain 5 frauds.
1. Calculate precision@5 and recall@5.
2. Calculate precision@10 and recall@10.
3. How many extra reviews and extra frauds result from increasing capacity from 5 to 10?
4. Each review costs $2. What is the additional review cost per additional fraud found?
 Assume all reviewed cases receive correct investigation outcomes. Do not assume investigation
 automatically prevents the loss.

interpretationPages.title: Precision@K and Recall@K
interpretationPages.text:
Precision@K and Recall@K

   M12 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Expanding the queue lowers precision from 60% to 50% but increases fraud coverage from
 37.5% to 62.5%. The extra cases may be worth reviewing, but the institution must have
 capacity and a useful intervention. Higher precision alone is not the objective.
 Why these steps matter
 Use the difference in fraud discoveries to assess the added five reviews. Dividing incremental
 spending by all five frauds in the expanded queue would over-credit discoveries already made by
 the smaller queue.

exercises.title: Compare With Random Review
exercises.question:
A batch contains 1,000 transactions and 20 frauds. The top 50 model-ranked transactions
 contain 15 frauds.
 Calculate:
1. Fraud prevalence and precision@50.
2. Lift@50: precision@50 divided by fraud prevalence.
3. Cumulative gain: the share of all frauds found in the top 50.
4. The expected number of frauds in a randomly selected set of 50 transactions.
 What percentage of the transaction population is reviewed? Explain what “15 times better”
 would mean here—and what it would not mean.

solutionPages.text:
Lift and Gain

   M13 | Worked solution — Compare With Random Review

1. Prevalence: 20/1,000 = 2%.
2. Precision@50: 15/50 = 30%.
3. Lift: 30%/2% = 15.
4. Cumulative gain: 15/20 = 75% of all frauds.
5. Random-review expectation: 50(0.02) = 1 fraud, compared with the model’s 15 in this
   sample.
6. Population reviewed: 50/1,000 = 5%.

interpretationPages.title: Lift and Gain
interpretationPages.text:
Lift and Gain

   M13 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Reviewing the top 5% captures 75% of frauds, with 15 times the fraud concentration of
 random review. This is not a 15-fold profit increase; fraud value, review cost, and the ability to
 prevent or recover losses remain separate questions.
 Why these steps matter
 A random sample will not necessarily contain exactly the expected fraud count. The lift
 comparison uses its expected concentration, not a claim that every random sample produces
 the same result.
paragraphs: Lift and Gain

What the answer means Reviewing the top 5% captures 75% of frauds, with 15 times the fraud concentration of random review. solutionPages.text:
Calibration

   M14 | Worked solution — Do the Probabilities Match Outcomes?

1. Expected defaults: 100(0.05) = 5; 100(0.10) = 10; 100(0.20) = 20. Total 35.
2. Observed rates: 3/100 = 3%, 10/100 = 10%, and 30/100 = 30%. Total actual defaults 43.
3. Largest understatement: The high band predicts 20% but observes 30%: 10 percentage
   points, or 10 additional defaults.
4. Loss comparison:
                                                  Expected loss = 35(4,000) = $140,000.
                                                  Realized loss = 43(4,000) = $172,000.
      Difference: $32,000.
5. Plot (predicted, observed): (5%, 3%), (10%, 10%), (20%, 30%).

interpretationPages.title: Calibration
interpretationPages.text:
Calibration

   M14 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The highest band understates observed risk in this sample, affecting the expected-loss
 calculation. The sample does not establish a permanent calibration error; uncertainty, time
 stability, and larger validation samples still matter.
 Why these steps matter
 Mean probability times group size equals the sum of individual probabilities, so it is appropriate
 for the expected count. Individual loans still default or do not default; a probability is evaluated
 by frequencies across cases, not by demanding that every single outcome match it exactly.

formulaPages.text:
Brier Score

   M15 | Formula explained (1/1)

 Question: How far are the predicted probabilities from the actual 0/1 outcomes?
                                                             N
                                                         1 X

 Read it aloud: For each loan, subtract its actual binary outcome from its predicted probability,
 square that difference, add the squared differences, and divide by the number of loans.
 Squaring removes the sign and gives larger deviations more weight. Use probabilities as
 decimals, not whole-number percentages.
 This is the binary Brier-score convention with range 0 to 1. Lower is better on the same
 evaluated sample; zero requires every probability to match its realized label exactly.

interpretationPages.title: Brier Score
interpretationPages.text:
Brier Score

   M15 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The model has better average probability accuracy on these four loans than the constant
 baseline. 0.1125 is not an 11.25% default rate or dollar loss. One non-default on a 60%
 prediction does not, by itself, establish miscalibration; probability quality is assessed across cases.
 Why these steps matter
 For a non-default, the error is the probability assigned to default. For a default, it is one minus
 that probability in magnitude. Squaring and averaging produces a unitless scoring penalty, not
 money lost on the loans.

formulaPages.title: Log Loss
formulaPages.text:
Log Loss

   M16 | Formula explained (2/2)

 Why the logarithm matters
 A probability near 1 for the actual outcome gives a penalty near 0. A probability near 0 for the
 actual outcome gives a very large penalty.
 For a legitimate transaction, use the model’s probability of legitimacy, one minus its fraud
 probability. Using the fraud probability directly would score the wrong event.
 Natural logs give a unitless score conventionally measured in nats. This is not a loss in dollars.
 An actual outcome assigned probability zero has unbounded log penalty; all supplied values here
 are strictly between 0 and 1.

interpretationPages.title: Log Loss
interpretationPages.text:
Log Loss

   M16 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Model A’s 99% fraud probability on a legitimate transaction receives a much larger penalty than
 B’s 60%. Identical classification accuracy can conceal very different probability quality.
 Log loss is not a dollar-cost calculation.
 Why these steps matter
 Both models make the same yes/no decisions at 0.50, but the more confident mistake puts
 much less probability on the true outcome. Log loss detects that difference because it evaluates
 the full probabilities rather than only the thresholded labels.

exercises.title: Check Economics and Capacity
exercises.question:
Two thresholds are evaluated on the same 20 frauds:
   Threshold                                                  TP                            FP          FN
   A                                                           15                            35           5
   B                                                           18                            82           2

 Each missed fraud costs $500. Each false alert costs $4. For this simplified cost model, other
 outcomes have zero incremental cost.
                                                  Error cost = 500(F N ) + 4(F P ).
 The team can review 75 alerts per day; every flag requires review.
 Calculate each threshold’s cost and review volume. Which has the lower modeled cost? Which
 is feasible with the existing team? State what must change before selecting the other operating
 point.

solutionPages.title: Expected Cost
solutionPages.text:
Expected Cost

   M17a | Worked solution — Check Economics and Capacity

1. Threshold A:
                                                  5(500) + 35(4) = 2,500 + 140 = $2,640.
2. Threshold B:
                                                  2(500) + 82(4) = 1,000 + 328 = $1,328.
3. Modeled savings from B: 2,640 − 1,328 = $1,312.
4. Review volumes: A produces 15 + 35 = 50 alerts; B produces 18 + 82 = 100.
5. Apply the capacity limit: A fits within 75; B exceeds capacity by 25 alerts.

interpretationPages.title: Expected Cost
interpretationPages.text:
Expected Cost

   M17a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 B has lower modeled error cost but is not feasible under the stated review policy. A is the
 feasible choice among these two today. B requires additional capacity or a separately tested
 workflow—not an assumption that unreviewed alerts still prevent fraud.
 Why these steps matter
 A lower computed cost assumes the required interventions can be delivered. Once the review
 queue exceeds capacity, the loss calculation is no longer enough to justify that operating point.
 Unreviewed alerts must not be credited as prevented fraud.

Threshold Economics

   M17b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Under this loss table, flagging becomes preferable above about 0.79%, not 50%. This is a
 classroom optimum for the stated assumptions; adding review costs, imperfect intervention,
 customer harm, or capacity constraints changes the decision.
 Why these steps matter
 A cost-based threshold can be far below 50% because the penalties are unequal. The calculation
 depends on calibrated probabilities and the assumed effectiveness of flagging. It does not
 establish a universal threshold for fraud detection.

learning.scenario: Choose between passing and flagging a transaction with calibrated fraud probability p. Passing fraud incurs a loss; flagging a legitimate transaction incurs a cost. Correct actions have zero incremental cost, and flagging fully prevents fraud loss.
learning.task: Find the probability where the two expected costs are equal. Calculate pass and flag costs for each listed probability. Ignore capacity and other costs for this exercise.
learning.interpretation: The break-even threshold follows from the supplied loss table and effective intervention assumption. Review costs, imperfect prevention or capacity constraints would change the decision.
learning.summary: Break-even probability: {threshold}. Pass costs: {pass}. Flag costs: {review}.

labels.cFP: Cost of flagging a legitimate transaction ($)

threshold.title: Break-even fraud probability
hints: Set cFN × p = cFP × (1 − p), giving p = cFP / (cFN + cFP).

pass.title: Expected passing costs
hints: Multiply each fraud probability by the missed-fraud loss.

review.title: Expected flagging costs
hints: Multiply each probability of legitimacy, 1 − p, by the false-alert cost.

readAloud: Passing costs cFN × p in expectation. Flagging costs cFP × (1 − p). Equating them gives the threshold cFP / (cFN + cFP). Below the threshold passing is cheaper; above it flagging is cheaper. The two actions have equal modeled cost at the threshold.
workedExplanation: Under this loss table, flagging becomes preferable above about 0.79%, not 50%. This is a classroom optimum for the stated assumptions; adding review costs, imperfect intervention, customer harm, or capacity constraints changes the decision.

A cost-based threshold can be far below 50% because the penalties are unequal. The calculation depends on calibrated probabilities and the assumed effectiveness of flagging. It does not establish a universal threshold for fraud detection.
workedArithmetic: At p = 0.005: pass cost = 500 × 0.005 = $2.50; flag cost = 4 × 0.995 = $3.98. Passing is cheaper.
At p = 0.01: pass cost = $5; flag cost = $3.96. At p = 0.10: pass cost = $50; flag cost = $3.60. Flagging is cheaper in both cases.

interpretationPages.title: Multi-Class F1
interpretationPages.text:
Multi-Class F1

   M18 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The classifier catches none of the negative statements. Micro-F1 and weighted-F1 conceal
 more of that weakness because neutral examples dominate. Here micro-F1 equals accuracy,
 11/16, because every record has exactly one label.
 Why these steps matter
 A wrong neutral-to-negative prediction adds a false negative to neutral and a false positive to
 negative. The same record therefore appears in two pooled error counts. Micro-F1 accounts for
 that convention; it must not be calculated by simply averaging the class F1 scores.

Fairness Diagnostics

   M19 | Worked solution — Compare Rates, Not Just Counts

1. Approval rates: A = 600/1,000 = 60%; B = 400/1,000 = 40%. B/A ratio
   = 40/60 = 0.667.
2. Repayment TPRs: A = 560/800 = 70%; B = 300/500 = 60%. Gap = 10 percentage
   points.
3. Non-repayers: A = 1,000 − 800 = 200; B = 1,000 − 500 = 500.
4. Non-repayers approved: A = 600 − 560 = 40; B = 400 − 300 = 100.
5. False-positive rates: A = 40/200 = 20%; B = 100/500 = 20%.

interpretationPages.title: Fairness Diagnostics
interpretationPages.text:
Fairness Diagnostics

   M19 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Approval rates and repayer capture differ even though both groups have the same FPR. These

 fairness, unfairness, or a legal conclusion. Outcome definitions, population differences, and
 uncertainty remain important.
 Why these steps matter
 The two groups have different repayment prevalences in the supplied benchmark. Equal FPR
 alone therefore does not imply equal approval rates or equal TPR. The arithmetic describes the
 pattern, not its cause or whether any decision is legally justified.

TPRA.title: Group A repayer true-positive rate
hints: Divide approved repayers in A by all repayers in A.

TPRB.title: Group B repayer true-positive rate

gap.title: Absolute repayer TPR gap
hints: Take the absolute difference between the two TPRs.

FPRA.title: Group A non-repayer false-positive rate
hints: Subtract approved repayers from approvals; divide by applicants minus repayers in A.

FPRB.title: Group B non-repayer false-positive rate
hints: Use the corresponding non-repayer counts for B.

readAloud: Calculate approvals among all applicants, approved repayers among all repayers, and approved non-repayers among all non-repayers. Here the positive decision is approval and the positive actual outcome is repayment. That differs from the fraud-positive convention used in most earlier exercises.

Subtract the repayer approval rates. This is a rate gap; multiply the decimal difference by 100 to state it in percentage points. The selection-rate ratio is a quotient, not a difference. It uses A as the reference group because the problem specifies B/A. The exercise is retrospective with known outcomes for every case. These diagnostics describe differences; no standalone legal or causal conclusion follows from the arithmetic.
workedExplanation: Approval rates and repayer capture differ even though both groups have the same FPR. These diagnostics identify differences that need investigation; they do not independently establish fairness, unfairness, or a legal conclusion. Outcome definitions, population differences, and uncertainty remain important.

The two groups have different repayment prevalences in the supplied benchmark. Equal FPR alone therefore does not imply equal approval rates or equal TPR. The arithmetic describes the pattern, not its cause or whether any decision is legally justified.
workedArithmetic: Approval rates: A = 600/1,000 = 60%; B = 400/1,000 = 40%. B/A selection-rate ratio = 0.40/0.60 ≈ 0.667.
Repayer TPRs: A = 560/800 = 70%; B = 300/500 = 60%; gap = 10 percentage points.
A has 1,000 − 800 = 200 non-repayers and 600 − 560 = 40 approved non-repayers, so FPR = 40/200 = 20%.
B has 1,000 − 500 = 500 non-repayers and 400 − 300 = 100 approved non-repayers, so FPR = 100/500 = 20%.

solutionPages.title: MAE
solutionPages.text:
MAE

   M20 | Worked solution — How Many Dollars Was the Forecast Off?

1. Model absolute errors: |100 − 90| = 10, |120 − 130| = 10, |80 − 100| = 20,
   |150 − 140| = 10.
2. Model MAE: (10 + 10 + 20 + 10)/4 = 12.5 thousand dollars.
3. Baseline absolute errors: 0, 20, 20, 50.
4. Baseline MAE: (0 + 20 + 20 + 50)/4 = 22.5 thousand dollars.
5. Improvement: 22.5 − 12.5 = 10 thousand dollars; relative reduction = 10/22.5 = 44.44%.

interpretationPages.title: MAE
interpretationPages.text:
MAE

   M20 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The model misses actual settlement outflow by $12,500 per day on average, versus $22,500
 for the baseline in this sample. The smaller miss is not automatically an equal dollar saving:
 MAE measures forecast error, not funding cost. It also does not show whether the forecast was
 too high or too low.
 Why these steps matter
 Using absolute differences stops overforecasts and underforecasts from cancelling each other.
 The mean remains in the financial target’s units, which makes it interpretable. It does not
 distinguish the funding consequences of a shortage from those of excess cash.

interpretationPages.title: RMSE
interpretationPages.text:
RMSE

   M21 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 B has the smaller average absolute miss—$7,500 versus $10,000—but a $30,000
 underforecast on one day. RMSE ranks A better because it gives large misses more weight.
 RMSE itself does not distinguish shortages from excess cash; the sign and funding consequences
 require separate attention.
 Why these steps matter
 The root does not undo the greater weight given to large errors; averaging occurs after squaring
 and before taking the root. A US$30,000 underforecast contributes nine times the squared
 penalty of a US$10,000 miss.

solutionPages.text:
Scaled Forecast Errors

   M22 | Worked solution — Percentage of What?

1. Absolute test errors: [10, 10, 20, 10]; sum = 50; test MAE = 50/4 = 12.5.
2. Percentage errors: 10/100 = 10%; 10/120 = 8.333%; 20/80 = 25%; 10/150 = 6.667%.
                      M AP E = (10 + 8.333 + 25 + 6.667)/4 = 12.5%.
3. Aggregate scale: W AP E = 50/(100 + 120 + 80 + 150) = 11.11%.
4. Training naive scale: (|100 − 80| + |120 − 100| + |140 − 120|)/3 = 20.
5. MASE: 12.5/20 = 0.625.

interpretationPages.text:
Scaled Forecast Errors

   M22 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 MAPE averages each day’s percentage miss. WAPE compares total absolute error with total
 volume. MASE says the test error is 62.5% of the training naive-error scale; it does not, by
 itself, establish superiority to a naive forecast on the test period. MAPE is undefined at zero
 actuals.
 Why these steps matter
 The denominators intentionally differ. MAPE gives each day’s proportional miss equal weight;
 WAPE evaluates error relative to total volume; MASE compares against a historical forecasting
 scale. A name containing “percentage” is not permission to ignore zeros, signs, or the
 evaluation window.

interpretationPages.text:
R2

   M23 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The model removes 73.83% of squared error relative to the sample-mean reference. It does
 not mean 73.83% of forecasts are correct. The test-set mean is an evaluation reference—not a
 forecast treasury could know before those outcomes occurred.
 Why these steps matter
 The 73.83% interpretation refers to a reduction in squared-error total, not a share of exactly
 correct forecasts. A forecast can receive a positive R-squared without matching any daily actual
 exactly.

solutionPages.text:
Prediction Intervals

   M24 | Worked solution — Covered, but Useful?

1. Original coverage: days 1, 3, 4, and 5 are inside; day 2 is outside. Coverage = 4/5 = 80%.
2. Original widths: 30, 20, 20, 30, 10. Mean = 110/5 = $22 million.
3. Widened intervals: [80, 130], [90, 130], [75, 115], [120, 170], [90, 120].
4. Widened coverage: all five actuals are inside, so 5/5 = 100%.
5. Widened average width: each interval grows by 20; 22 + 20 = $42 million.

interpretationPages.title: Prediction Intervals
interpretationPages.text:
Prediction Intervals

   M24 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Wider ranges cover more outcomes but give less precise funding guidance. Neither result alone
 determines the better system: treasury needs sufficiently reliable coverage and useful width.
 Five observations are too few to conclude that the original 90% intervals are systematically
 miscalibrated.
 Why these steps matter
 Making every interval very wide can raise coverage without giving treasury a useful forecast.
 Coverage and width must be read together, and the five-day count alone is too small to
 establish long-run calibration.

solutionPages.title: Pinball Loss
solutionPages.text:
Pinball Loss

   M25 | Worked solution — Penalize a Cash Shortage More Heavily

1. Actual 150: forecast is short by 150 − 130 = 20; loss = 0.95(20) = 19.
2. Actual 120: forecast is high by 130 − 120 = 10; loss = 0.05(10) = 0.5.
3. Actual 130: no error; loss = 0.
4. Average: (19 + 0.5 + 0)/3 = 6.5, in weighted $ million error units.
5. Equal-sized misses: a 10-unit shortage costs 0.95(10) = 9.5 score units; a 10-unit excess
   costs 0.05(10) = 0.5. Ratio = 9.5/0.5 = 19.

interpretationPages.title: Pinball Loss
interpretationPages.text:
Pinball Loss

   M25 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 This scoring rule strongly discourages underestimating a high liquidity quantile. The 19-to-1
 weighting comes from choosing the 95th percentile; it is not automatically the bank’s actual
 funding-cost ratio. The computed score is not a realized cash loss.
 Why these steps matter
 The high quantile intentionally penalizes shortfalls more than excess. The weights describe the
 scoring target, not observed borrowing fees or a stated regulatory reserve requirement. The
 average 6.5 is in weighted million-dollar error units, not realized loss.

interpretationPages.title: Silhouette
interpretationPages.text:
Silhouette

   M26 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 A is closer to its own segment. B lies near a segment boundary. C is, on average, closer to
 another segment than to its assigned one, so its assignment needs inspection. The near-zero
 mean suggests weak separation for these customers. None of these values demonstrates that the
 segments improve marketing response, retention, or profitability.
 Why these steps matter
 Positive, zero, and negative values indicate different geometric relationships. Those signs do not
 mean profitable, neutral, and unprofitable customers. Geometry is only one part of validating
 whether a segmentation is useful.

   M27a | Worked solution — When Does Another Segment Stop Helping?

1. One cluster: centroid = (1 + 2 + 8 + 9)/4 = 5.
            I1 = (1 − 5)2 + (2 − 5)2 + (8 − 5)2 + (9 − 5)2 = 16 + 9 + 9 + 16 = 50.
2. Two clusters: centroids 1.5 and 8.5.
                               I2 = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1.
3. Three clusters: centroids 1.5, 8, 9.
                                 I3 = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0 + 0 = 0.5.
4. Reductions: 50 − 1 = 49, then 1 − 0.5 = 0.5. The apparent elbow is k = 2.

interpretationPages.title: Inertia
interpretationPages.text:
Inertia

   M27a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Two groups explain most of the variation here: lower and higher savings. A third adds little
 compactness. Inertia uses squared feature units, not dollars of business value; it also cannot
 establish stability or usefulness. Giving every customer a separate cluster would produce zero
 inertia but no meaningful segmentation.
 Why these steps matter
 The squared distances quantify compactness on the chosen scale. Dividing a group into smaller
 groups can reduce the total even if no useful business distinction is added, so the minimum
 inertia alone is not a defensible stopping rule.

interpretationPages.title: Adjusted Rand Index
interpretationPages.text:
Adjusted Rand Index

   M27b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 These two runs disagree substantially on who belongs together; agreement is below the
 chance-adjusted reference for these cluster sizes. The value is not “negative accuracy.” Cluster
 names are arbitrary: exchanging X and Y would leave ARI unchanged. This small exercise does
 not establish stability for the bank’s full customer population.
 Why these steps matter
 Compute pair counts, not percentages of matching letters. A relabeling can change every
 displayed group name without moving any customer. ARI therefore ignores names and compares
 the underlying grouping structure.

   M28 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Both questions have an evidence “hit,” but Q1 is missing half its required source material. A
 100% question-level hit rate is not 100% relevant-chunk recall. Two-thirds of the
 supplied context is irrelevant in both cases. Generation still needs separate evaluation.
 Why these steps matter
 The missing B chunk in Q1 matters even though A was retrieved. Counting Q1 as a binary
 “hit” discards information about completeness. Mean recall across questions also differs from
 pooling all retrieved chunks into one global numerator and denominator.

learning.task: Calculate recall and context precision per question, then the unweighted mean of each across questions.
learning.interpretation: Finding one relevant passage is a hit, but may leave required evidence missing. Averaging per-query recall is different from pooling all passage counts. Answer quality needs its own evaluation.
learning.summary: Mean retrieval recall: {meanRecall}; mean context precision: {meanPrecision}.

labels.relevant: All relevant passages available per question

recalls.title: Recall for each question
hints: Divide relevant passages retrieved by all relevant passages available for that question.

precision.title: Context precision for each question
hints: Divide relevant passages retrieved by K.

meanRecall.title: Mean retrieval recall
hints: Average the per-question recall fractions.

meanPrecision.title: Mean context precision
hints: Average the per-question context-precision fractions.

readAloud: Count retrieved chunks that are relevant. Divide by all relevant chunks for recall; divide by the retrieved queue size for context precision. Compute each question separately, then take an unweighted average across questions. Here each query retrieves exactly three distinct chunks. Context precision uses simple relevant-chunk share in this exercise, not a rank-weighted evaluator’s definition.
workedExplanation: Both questions have an evidence “hit,” but Q1 is missing half its required source material. A 100% question-level hit rate is not 100% relevant-chunk recall. Two-thirds of the supplied context is irrelevant in both cases. Generation still needs separate evaluation.

The missing B chunk in Q1 matters even though A was retrieved. Counting Q1 as a binary “hit” discards information about completeness. Mean recall across questions also differs from pooling all retrieved chunks into one global numerator and denominator.
workedArithmetic: Q1 retrieves one of its two relevant passages: recall = 1/2 = 50%; context precision = 1/3 ≈ 33.33%.
Q2 retrieves its only relevant passage: recall = 1/1 = 100%; context precision = 1/3 ≈ 33.33%.

solutionPages.title: MRR
solutionPages.text:
MRR

   M29a | Worked solution — How Soon Does the First Useful Source Appear?

1. Reciprocal ranks: Q1 = 1; Q2 = 1/2 = 0.5; Q3 = 1/4 = 0.25; Q4 = 0.
2. Original MRR:
                                                  (1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0)/4 = 1.75/4 = 0.4375.
3. Updated Q4 contribution: 1/2 = 0.5.
4. Updated MRR:
                                                  (1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.5)/4 = 2.25/4 = 0.5625.
5. Improvement: 0.5625 − 0.4375 = 0.125 score units.

interpretationPages.title: MRR
interpretationPages.text:
MRR

   M29a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The first useful passage now appears earlier for more questions, reducing how far an analyst or
 downstream system must search. MRR is not the percentage of correct answers and ignores
 the ordering of additional relevant passages after the first.
 Why these steps matter
 The unresolved question belongs in the denominator of the original MRR. Dropping it would
 inflate the reported retrieval quality by evaluating only successful searches.

solutionPages.text:
nDCG

   M29b | Worked solution — Put the Best Evidence First

1. Convert relevance to gain: 21 − 1 = 1, 23 − 1 = 7, 20 − 1 = 0.
2. Actual order:
                                                  DCG = 1/1 + 7/1.585 + 0/2 ≈ 5.4165.
3. Ideal order: grades [3, 1, 0], gains [7, 1, 0].
                             IDCG = 7/1 + 1/1.585 + 0/2 ≈ 7.6309.
4. Normalize:
                                                  nDCG@3 = 5.4165/7.6309 ≈ 0.7098.

interpretationPages.title: nDCG
interpretationPages.text:
nDCG

   M29b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The retriever found the strongest passage but put it behind weaker evidence. Its discounted
 relevance score is about 71% of the ideal ordering’s score. Moving the grade-3 passage first
 gives nDCG of 1 here. Neither score establishes that the generated answer uses the passage
 correctly.
 Why these steps matter
 The normalized result is a fraction of ideal discounted relevance, not the fraction of sources
 that are relevant. Ranking the strongest source second loses more credit under exponential gain
 than a simple relevant-versus-irrelevant count would reveal.

exercises.title: Three Checks, Three Denominators
exercises.question:
The retrieved evidence says:
▶ A: Revenue was $100 million in 2024 and $120 million in 2025.
▶ B: 2025 net profit was $12 million.
▶ C: 2025 debt was $40 million.

The generated answer makes five claims:
1. “2025 revenue was $120 million.” [A]
2. “Revenue grew 20%.” [A]
3. “2025 net profit was $12 million.” [C]
4. “2025 debt was $30 million.” [C]
5. “Debt will fall next year.” No citation.
 Calculate faithfulness over five claims, citation correctness over four claim–citation pairs, and
 numerical accuracy over the four financial figures: 120, 20%, 12, and 30. Faithfulness permits
 support from any retrieved passage; citation correctness requires the attached source to support
 that claim.

interpretationPages.title: Sharpe and Sortino
interpretationPages.text:
Sharpe and Sortino

   M31 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 B’s higher return came with more risk. It does not win on either risk-adjusted ratio here. A
 Sharpe ratio of 0.50 means half a unit of excess return per unit of measured volatility—not a
 50% return or a 50% chance of profit. These estimates do not establish future performance or
 tail safety.
 Why these steps matter
 The numerator rewards performance above the specified reference. The denominator identifies
 the kind of variability being charged against that performance. B’s extra return is not enough to
 overcome its larger total volatility on Sharpe, while both funds have the same return per unit of
 supplied downside deviation.

interpretationPages.title: Maximum Drawdown
interpretationPages.text:
Maximum Drawdown

   M32a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 An investor ended up 25% but first endured a one-third decline from the account’s earlier peak.
 Final return hides that path. The later value of 125 cannot be used as the peak for the earlier
 decline to 80.
 Why these steps matter

 125. The numerator measures the investor’s decline from that peak. A strong final return
 cannot remove the funding or behavioral strain experienced during the earlier drawdown.

solutionPages.title: Turnover and Constraints
solutionPages.text:
Turnover and Constraints

   M32b | Worked solution — Can the Allocation Be Implemented?

1. Weight changes: [−20, +10, +10] percentage points.
2. One-way turnover: (20 + 10 + 10)/2 = 20%, equivalent to $200,000 on one side.
3. Trades: sell $200,000 of A; buy $100,000 of B and $100,000 of C. Gross traded value
   = $400, 000.
4. Cost: 400,000 × 0.001 = $400. Costs apply to both purchases and sales, not just one-way
   turnover.
5. Constraint check: [40, 40, 20]% is feasible. The alternative has one violation: A exceeds its
   50% cap by 5 percentage points, or $50,000.

interpretationPages.title: Turnover and Constraints
interpretationPages.text:
Turnover and Constraints

   M32b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Turnover estimates the trading burden; the fee calculation depends on the stated convention. A
 mandatory allocation cap is a separate pass/fail condition. Better expected performance does
 not make a noncompliant proposed allocation feasible.
 Why these steps matter
 Selling 20% of portfolio value and reinvesting it creates 20% one-way turnover but 40% gross
 trading. The stated fee charges both sides. Likewise, an asset at 55% breaches a 50% cap by
 five percentage points, not by 5% of its current holding.

Tracking Error

   M32c | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Tracking error describes the variability of benchmark-relative returns—not a 4% loss or 4%
 underperformance. Mean monthly active return is zero here, yet active risk is positive.
 Annualization and this four-observation estimate should not be treated as reliable without more
 data.
 Why these steps matter
 Active returns of +1 and −1 percentage point average to zero but still fluctuate. Tracking error
 measures that fluctuation. Computing the standard deviation of the fund’s returns alone would
 answer a different question about total risk rather than benchmark-relative risk.

solutionPages.title: VaR and Expected Shortfall
solutionPages.text:
VaR and Expected Shortfall

   M33 | Worked solution — Threshold versus Tail Average

1. Sort losses: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 20].
2. Locate VaR: ⌈0.80 × 10⌉ = 8. The eighth loss is 7.
                                 V aR80%,1 day = $7, 000.
3. Identify the tail: worst 20% × 10 = 2 scenarios have losses 10 and 20.
                             ES80%,1 day = (10 + 20)/2 = $15, 000.
4. Strict exceedances: 10 and 20 exceed 7, so 2/10 = 20%.

interpretationPages.title: VaR and Expected Shortfall
interpretationPages.text:
VaR and Expected Shortfall

   M33 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Under this empirical scenario distribution, 80% of one-day losses are no more than $7,000; the
 worst fifth averages $15,000. VaR is not a maximum loss: even this tiny sample includes a
 $20,000 loss. The 80% level is a teaching choice, not a recommended risk policy.
 Why these steps matter
 VaR identifies where the tail begins under the chosen convention. Expected Shortfall describes
 the size of losses within that tail. They can differ considerably because the threshold does not
 reveal how far the worst observations extend beyond it. Both are conditional on the supplied
 scenario distribution.

interpretationPages.title: Monte Carlo Error
interpretationPages.text:
Monte Carlo Error

   M34 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Quadrupling independent runs halves simulation noise. It does not validate assumed default
 probabilities, recoveries, or correlations. This interval describes uncertainty in the estimated
 probability conditional on the specified simulation model, not uncertainty about whether
 that model is realistic.
 Why these steps matter
 A single run says breach or no breach. More runs make the average of those binary outcomes
 more stable. With the probability held fixed, multiplying run count by four divides its standard
 error by two because the denominator enters under a square root. It does not halve uncertainty
 about whether the financial assumptions are correct.

newSE.title: Standard error with the new run count
hints: Keep p unchanged and replace N by the new run count in the standard-error formula.

readAloud: Divide breach runs by total runs. Multiply that estimated fraction by its complement, divide by run count, and take the square root. Add and subtract 1.96 standard errors for the stated normal approximation. Runs are independent, equally weighted, and generated under one fixed simulation model. This approximation is not suitable for every very small or near-zero/near-one breach sample.
workedExplanation: Quadrupling independent runs halves simulation noise. It does not validate assumed default probabilities, recoveries, or correlations. This interval describes uncertainty in the estimated probability conditional on the specified simulation model, not uncertainty about whether that model is realistic.

A single run says breach or no breach. More runs make the average of those binary outcomes more stable. With the probability held fixed, multiplying run count by four divides its standard error by two because the denominator enters under a square root. It does not halve uncertainty about whether the financial assumptions are correct.
workedArithmetic: At 10,000 runs, SE = √(0.09/10,000) = 0.003, or 0.3 percentage points.

exercises.title: Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?
exercises.question:
A bank evaluates a 99% one-day VaR forecast over 250 trading days. Actual daily losses
 exceed that day’s predicted VaR on 10 days. Six of those exceptions occur within one 10-day
 period.
 Calculate:
1. The observed exception rate.
2. The nominal expected number of exceptions under the 99% target.
3. The ratio of observed to nominal exception rates.
 Explain why reviewing only the annual exception count would miss something important. Does
 the count alone identify the cause of the problem?

solutionPages.title: VaR Exceptions
solutionPages.text:
VaR Exceptions

   M35 | Worked solution — Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?

1. Observed exception rate: 10/250 = 4%.
2. Nominal exception probability: 1 − 0.99 = 1%.
3. Expected count: 250(0.01) = 2.5 exceptions—not a guaranteed count or an acceptance
   band.
4. Rate ratio: 4%/1% = 4× the nominal rate.
5. Timing: six exceptions concentrated in ten days can reveal a stress-period weakness hidden
   by an annual average.
paragraphs: VaR Exceptions
M35 | Worked solution — Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?

interpretationPages.title: VaR Exceptions
interpretationPages.text:
VaR Exceptions

   M35 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The model’s tail forecast deserves investigation: exceptions are more frequent than its nominal
 target, and many are clustered. Frequency tests, dependence checks, breach sizes, and market
 or data changes are needed to assess the problem. The count alone does not prove a particular
 cause or quantify losses beyond VaR.
 Why these steps matter
 Using the daily matching forecast matters: comparing every day against one convenient
 annual-average VaR would change the test. The nominal 1% rate follows from the 99% target;
 it does not explain why this sample’s observed rate is 4% or why six exceptions appeared close
 together.

solutionPages.title: Reward and Regret
solutionPages.text:
Reward and Regret

   M36 | Worked solution — Better Than the Baseline, Short of Hindsight

1. Policy total cost: 300 + 200 + 400 = $900.
2. Cumulative reward: −300 − 200 − 400 = −$900 in the chosen reward units.
3. Improvement over TWAP: 1,200 − 900 = $300.
4. Hindsight regret: 900 − 700 = $200.
5. One basis point of this order: 1,000,000 × 0.0001 = $100. Improvement
   = 300/100 = 3 bps; regret = 200/100 = 2 bps.

interpretationPages.title: Reward and Regret
interpretationPages.text:
Reward and Regret

   M36 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The policy saves 3 basis points versus TWAP but costs 2 basis points more than the hindsight
 schedule. Hindsight has information the live policy did not possess. A less negative reward is
 better here; reward becomes economically misleading if material costs or incomplete-order
 penalties are omitted.
 Why these steps matter
 The policy can beat a realistic baseline while still falling short of hindsight. Those are different
 comparisons and should not be combined. The order-value denominator turns dollar differences
 into comparable cost fractions, while the reward sign convention determines which numerical
 direction is better.

exercises.title: Completed, Checked, and Within Authority?
exercises.question:
An invoice agent processes 100 assigned tasks:
▶ 90 complete correctly and pass every required verification check.
▶ 95 pass the required field checks; five of these do not finish the workflow.
▶ Four tasks contain an attempted action outside the agent’s authority. Every such attempt is
  blocked.
▶ Across 200 tool calls, 10 return an error.
 Define success as correct completion plus all required checks. Calculate task success,
 field-verification pass rate, task-level unsafe-attempt rate, task-level unsafe-execution rate,
 and tool-call error rate. Does blocking all unsafe attempts make those attempts irrelevant?

solutionPages.title: PSI
solutionPages.text:
PSI

   M38 | Worked solution — Has the Applicant Mix Changed?

1. Lower-risk band:
                 (0.20 − 0.50) ln(0.20/0.50) = (−0.30)(−0.9163) = 0.27489.
2. Higher-risk band:
                   (0.80 − 0.50) ln(0.80/0.50) = (0.30)(0.4700) = 0.14100.
3. Total: P SI = 0.27489 + 0.14100 = 0.41589.
4. Describe the actual shift: the higher-risk band rose from 50% to 80%, a
   30-percentage-point increase.

interpretationPages.title: PSI
interpretationPages.text:
PSI

   M38 | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The score distribution has changed. Investigate applicant channels, product mix, policy changes,
 and the data pipeline. PSI is not an accuracy score or a default-rate estimate; outcome labels
 are needed to assess prediction quality. Identical band shares would give PSI of zero, but zero
 PSI would not guarantee a sound model.
 Why these steps matter
 For the lower band, both the share change and the log ratio are negative, producing a positive
 contribution. For the higher band, both are positive. The sum records the distribution change
 without establishing that predictions became wrong or that default rates actually rose.

exercises.title: The Average Can Pass While the Service Fails
exercises.question:
A fraud-scoring service handles 100 requests, with eventual response times:
   Requests                                            Latency each
   95                                                  40 ms
   4                                                   180 ms
   1                                                   1,000 ms

 Calculate mean latency, p95, and p99. Use the nearest-rank percentile: rank ⌈pN ⌉ in ascending
 order.
 The caller treats any response after 100 ms as a deadline failure, even if a result later arrives.
 Calculate this timeout/deadline-failure rate. The service objective requires 99% of requests
 within 100 ms. Does this sample meet it?

   M39a | Worked solution — The Average Can Pass While the Service Fails

1. Total latency: 95(40) + 4(180) + 1(1,000) = 3,800 + 720 + 1,000 = 5,520 ms.
2. Mean: 5,520/100 = 55.2 ms.

5. Deadline failures: 4 + 1 = 5 requests; 5/100 = 5%. Only 95% finish within 100 ms.

interpretationPages.text:

   M39a | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 The mean and p95 look fast, but the 99%-within-100-ms objective is missed. Five payment

 The 95 fast requests dominate the average and determine p95. The next four requests
 determine p99 and create deadline failures along with the slowest request. Averaging the three
 latency values without their request counts would give each group the wrong weight.

solutionPages.title: Throughput and Review Load
solutionPages.text:
Throughput and Review Load

   M39b | Worked solution — Calculate Both Bottlenecks

1. API capacity: 12,000/60 = 200 requests/second.
2. API backlog growth: 250 − 200 = 50 requests/second.
3. Ten-minute backlog: 50 × 10 × 60 = 30, 000 requests.
4. Daily human capacity: 15 × 20 = 300 cases.
5. Daily unworked alerts: 500 − 300 = 200. After three days: 200(3) = 600 alerts.
6. Required analyst pace: 500/15 = 33.33 cases/day, versus the available 20.

interpretationPages.title: Throughput and Review Load
interpretationPages.text:
Throughput and Review Load

   M39b | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 There are two separate capacity failures: scoring cannot keep up with incoming payments, and
 investigators cannot work the generated queue. Increasing API capacity would not fix the review
 backlog. A threshold or staffing change must account for the fraud that would remain
 unreviewed.
 Why these steps matter
 A rate difference has units of requests per second or alerts per day. Multiplying by matching
 elapsed time produces a count. Keeping the units explicit prevents confusing 12,000 requests
 per minute with 12,000 per second, or interpreting a queue count as a response time.

Cost and Abstention

   M39c | Worked solution — Price the Entire Workflow

1. Abstention rate: 100/1,000 = 10%. Automated-answer coverage = 900/1,000 = 90%.
2. Human review cost: 100($3) = $300.
3. Total operating cost: $500 + $300 = $800.

5. Correctly resolved requests: 800 + 100 = 900.
                      All-in cost per correct resolution = 800/900 ≈ $0.89.
6. Automatic-answer accuracy: 800/900 = 88.89%.

interpretationPages.title: Cost and Abstention
interpretationPages.text:
Cost and Abstention

   M39c | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 Abstention adds review expense and routes those cases to correct manual resolution under the
 exercise’s assumptions. Model spend alone understates operating cost. Even the all-in $0.80 per
 request excludes the consequences of the 100 wrong answers; it is not a complete economic loss
 measure.
 Why these steps matter
 The same numerical fraction can represent different concepts: 800/900 is automatic-answer
 accuracy, while $800 divided by 900 correct resolutions is a cost in dollars. The numerator’s
 units and the denominator’s population determine the meaning. The scenario does not establish
 what automatic answers would have been produced on the abstained cases.

hints: Divide reviewed requests by incoming requests.

coverage.title: Automatic-answer coverage
hints: Divide incoming minus reviewed requests by incoming requests.

reviewSpend.title: Human review spending
hints: Multiply reviewed requests by cost per review.

totalCost.title: Total operating cost
hints: Add model/retrieval spending and human review spending.

perRequest.title: Cost per incoming request
hints: Divide total operating cost by incoming requests.

correct.title: Correctly resolved requests
hints: Add correct automatic answers and all reviewed requests.

perCorrect.title: Cost per correct resolution
hints: Divide total operating cost by correctly resolved requests.

autoAccuracy.title: Accuracy among automatic answers
hints: Divide correct automatic answers by incoming minus reviewed requests.

readAloud: Divide abstentions and automatic answers by incoming requests. Evaluate accuracy only among the requests actually answered automatically. Here every request takes exactly one of those routes, so N = Nabstain + Nauto . A decision to abstain is not automatically a wrong answer; it routes the case to the stated human process.

Add all model-and-retrieval spending to all required human review spending. Divide that same total either by incoming volume or by the number correctly resolved. Failed automatic answers remain in the spending numerator. All manually reviewed requests are correctly resolved under the supplied assumption. Downstream financial harm is explicitly excluded.
workedExplanation: Abstention adds review expense and routes those cases to correct manual resolution under the exercise’s assumptions. Model spend alone understates operating cost. Even the all-in $0.80 per request excludes the consequences of the 100 wrong answers; it is not a complete economic loss measure.

The same numerical fraction can represent different concepts: 800/900 is automatic-answer accuracy, while $800 divided by 900 correct resolutions is a cost in dollars. The numerator’s units and the denominator’s population determine the meaning. The scenario does not establish what automatic answers would have been produced on the abstained cases.
workedArithmetic: Cost per incoming request = $800/1,000 = $0.80. Correct resolutions = 800 + 100 = 900; cost per correct resolution = $800/900 ≈ $0.89.
Automatic-answer accuracy = 800/900 ≈ 88.89%. This shares the numerical fraction with cost per correct resolution but has different units and meaning.

solutionPages.title: Uptime
solutionPages.text:
Uptime

   M39d | Worked solution — Translate the Percentage into Minutes

1. Scheduled time: 30 × 24 × 60 = 43, 200 minutes.
2. Available time: 43,200 − 90 = 43,110 minutes.
3. Achieved availability:
                                                  43,110/43,200 × 100% = 99.7917%.
4. Allowed unavailability: 43,200(1 − 0.999) = 43.2 minutes.
5. Excess downtime: 90 − 43.2 = 46.8 minutes.

interpretationPages.title: Uptime
interpretationPages.text:
Uptime

   M39d | Interpretation

 What the answer means
 “Over 99% available” is not enough for the specified 99.9% objective. The service was
 unavailable for more than twice its allotted downtime. Time-based availability also does not
 reveal how many payment requests were affected or whether the outage coincided with peak
 demand.
 Why these steps matter
 A target of 99.9% leaves 0.1% of scheduled time for unavailability, not 0.9%. Multiplying that
 small fraction by the full month’s minutes makes the allowance concrete. The same outage
 length can affect very different payment volumes depending on when it occurs.

The same outage length can affect very different payment volumes depending on when it occurs.

learning.scenario: A service is scheduled continuously for the supplied number of days. Use time-based availability, not request-weighted success.
learning.task: Convert the scheduled period to minutes, calculate available minutes and availability, then compute downtime allowed by the objective and downtime beyond that allowance.
learning.interpretation: An availability percentage must be compared with its exact target. Time-based availability also does not reveal how many requests were affected or whether downtime coincided with peak demand.

hints: Subtract unavailable minutes from scheduled minutes.

hints: Divide available minutes by scheduled minutes.

allowed.title: Downtime allowed by the objective
hints: Multiply scheduled minutes by 1 − objective.

It does not weight downtime by how many requests arrived during each minute.

z.meaning: Combined model score, measured in log-odds rather than dollars or percentage points.

p or P D.meaning: Estimated probability of default within one year; enter it as a decimal.

DTI.meaning: Debt-to-income ratio: debt-payment burden relative to income on a consistent time basis. The supplied 35% is entered as 35, not 0.35.

D.meaning: Delinquency indicator: 1 means the specified prior late-payment condition occurred; 0 means it did not.
Number of days over which the alert backlog accumulates; three here.
Minutes when the service is completely unavailable, 90; D is downtime here, not a loan delinquency indicator.

I.meaning: Annual income in thousands of dollars; I = 60 means US$60,000, not US$60.

−3.meaning: Intercept: the starting score before feature contributions are added.

0.04, 1.2, −0.03.meaning: Fitted coefficients: score change for a one-unit increase in the corresponding input, holding others fixed.

e, e−z.meaning: Euler’s number, about 2.71828, raised to the negative score. Here e is not a forecast error.

Odds; log-odds.meaning: Odds are p/(1 − p); log-odds are the natural logarithm of the odds. The score z is on this scale.

EAD.meaning: Exposure at default: dollars outstanding when default occurs. Assume the full US$10,000 is exposed.

LGD.meaning: Loss given default: the fraction of exposure not recovered; 40% becomes 0.40.

EL.meaning: Expected loss: the model’s average loss across comparable loans, in dollars over the stated horizon.
Analytical expected portfolio loss under the supplied default and loss assumptions.

≥; review threshold.meaning: Greater than or equal to; the minimum estimated risk that triggers human review here.

Calibration.meaning: Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event rates across comparable cases.

Default.meaning: Failure to meet the repayment condition specified by the lender; the model predicts whether that event occurs within one year.

Feature; fitted coefficient.meaning: A supplied input describing an applicant; a numeric weight learned earlier from training examples and held fixed during this prediction.

G.meaning: Gini impurity: how mixed a node is; for two classes it ranges from 0 to 0.5.
Cumulative undiscounted reward across this execution episode; not a return percentage or probability.

pf , pl.meaning: Fractions of fraud and legitimate records within the particular node; they sum to 1.

p2f , p2l.meaning: Each class fraction multiplied by itself; the square is not a percentage conversion.

N.meaning: Number of records in the parent node: 10.
Number of equally weighted scenarios; 10 here.
Number of independent simulation runs; 2,500 initially and 10,000 in the comparison.
Incoming request count, 1,000; includes automatic answers and abstentions.

n1 , n2.meaning: Child record counts: 4 for new devices and 6 for trusted devices.

G 1 , G2.meaning: Impurities of the new-device and trusted-device child nodes.

Gparent , Gsplit.meaning: Original impurity and record-weighted impurity after the split.

∆G.meaning: Reduction in impurity; a positive value means the proposed split makes the training groups less mixed.

B, b.meaning: Number of trees, here 3, and an index selecting one tree.
Number of trees, here 3, and the index of an individual tree.

pb , pforest.meaning: One tree’s supplied fraud score and the mean score across trees.

Σ (b = 1 … B).meaning: Add the contribution from each of the B trees.

Challenge.meaning: An extra identity or transaction check; it is not necessarily a decline.

F0.meaning: Initial combined score, −2.0, before the two supplied trees contribute.

m.meaning: Tree or boosting-step number; m = 1 for the first tree and m = 2 for the second.
Number of scenarios in the selected tail, (1 − α)N = 2 here.

Fm−1 , Fm.meaning: Combined log-odds scores before and after adding tree m.

hm.meaning: Correction supplied by tree m for this applicant; the values are 0.8 and 0.4.

η (eta).meaning: Learning rate: fraction of each tree’s correction applied; compare 0.5 with 0.25.

p.meaning: Predicted default probability after the final tree, on a 0–1 scale.
Percentile fraction, 0.90 for p90 or 0.95 for p95.
Calibrated probability that the transaction is fraud, entered as a decimal.
Percentile fraction: 0.95 for p95 and 0.99 for p99.

e−Fm.meaning: Exponential of the negative final score; e ≈ 2.71828.

Log-odds.meaning: Natural logarithm of probability divided by one minus probability; not the probability itself.

Boosting.meaning: Adding models sequentially to improve the current prediction under a specified loss function.

K-means; K.meaning: A clustering method using a chosen number of centers; here K = 2.

xi , i.meaning: Savings rate of customer i; i identifies a customer, not an exponent.

µj (mu), j.meaning: Center, or centroid, of group j; j identifies one of the two groups.

dij.meaning: Distance from customer i to center j.

|xi − µj |.meaning: Absolute difference: remove the minus sign so distance cannot be negative.

nj.meaning: Number of customers currently assigned to group j.

Cluster; centroid.meaning: A group of similar observations; its center is the arithmetic average of the assigned values here.

Assignment; update.meaning: Choose a customer’s group; then recalculate each group’s center.

Unsupervised.meaning: The grouping uses input behavior without a supplied outcome label such as default.

Isolation path.meaning: The sequence of splits followed for an observation; its length counts the steps used to isolate it.

hb.meaning: Path length for this transaction in tree b.

h̄.meaning: Mean path length; the bar means average, not a new type of tree.

c.meaning: Positive normalization constant supplied as 4; scales path length for comparison.
Fixed loss per actual default, US$4,000.
Fee rate per dollar traded; 10 basis points equals 0.001.

s.meaning: Anomaly score with higher meaning more unusual; it is not fraud probability.

2u.meaning: Two raised to exponent u; a negative exponent produces a reciprocal, such as 2−1 = 1/2.

Rank.meaning: Position after sorting scores. Rank 1 is the transaction reviewed first here.

Anomaly.meaning: An observation that differs from the reference pattern; it can be legitimate.

ARIMA.meaning: A forecasting method with three ingredients: how current values relate to earlier values, how much values change from one period to the next, and how earlier forecast errors affect the next forecast. Its full name is Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average.

(1, 1, 0).meaning: The three model orders: one lag of the differenced series; difference once; no lagged-error term.

yt , yt−1.meaning: Today’s and yesterday’s actual settlement outflows, in millions of dollars.

t + 1, t + 2.meaning: One and two days beyond the last observed day; these are forecast horizons.

∆ (delta).meaning: Change operator: subtract the preceding value.

∆yt.meaning: Latest observed daily change, not the outflow level.

Δŷₜ₊₁.meaning: Predicted next change; the hat indicates a forecast.

ŷt+1 , ŷt+2.meaning: Predicted future outflow levels; obtain them by adding forecast changes.

0.5.meaning: Fitted autoregressive coefficient: this model carries half the latest change into the next prediction.

Drift; future error.meaning: A constant average-change term; an unpredictable future shock. No drift is added and future shocks have forecast mean zero here.

Buffer.meaning: Extra liquidity above the point forecast; the fixed US$10 million is an assumption, not a prediction interval.

Absolute error.meaning: Magnitude of actual minus forecast, written |y − ŷ|; the sign is removed.

Naive forecast.meaning: A simple reference prediction; the last-value version sets tomorrow equal to today’s level.

Node; u, v.meaning: One entity in the network, such as an account, device, or merchant; u and v denote selected nodes.

Edge.meaning: One link between two entities; the supplied list defines all links available at the cutoff.

N (v).meaning: Set of nodes directly linked to node v; read as “neighbors of v.”

|N (v)|.meaning: Number of elements in that set; vertical bars around a set mean its size, not absolute value.

deg(v).meaning: Degree: number of direct links to node v in this simple graph.

Path.meaning: A route that follows one linked pair after another.

d(u, v).meaning: Shortest-path length between nodes u and v, counted in edges.

min.meaning: Choose the smallest value among the candidate path lengths.

Connected component.meaning: A maximal set of mutually reachable nodes; adding another reachable node would mean the set was incomplete.

Cutoff.meaning: Latest time at which a link is allowed into this historical decision; later links cannot be used.

Token.meaning: An input text unit. In this toy example each of the two words is treated as one token.

si.meaning: Already-scaled attention logit for token i; a raw score before normalization.
Customer-level silhouette score, normally between −1 and 1 for valid distances.

i, j.meaning: Token indices; j runs over all tokens in the softmax denominator.

e; ln.meaning: Exponential base, about 2.71828; its inverse, the natural logarithm. Thus eln(3) = 3.

ai.meaning: Nonnegative attention weight for token i; all attention weights sum to 1.
Mean distance from customer i to other customers in its assigned cluster; exclude the customer itself.

vi.meaning: Supplied scalar value associated with token i: −1 for “loss” and +1 for “narrowed.”

P.meaning: Add the indicated terms: token exponentials in the denominator or weighted token values in the representation.
Precision: the fraction of alerts that are genuine fraud; use 0.30 here.

h.meaning: Combined scalar representation after attention; a learned vector is simplified to one number here.

z + , z0 , z−.meaning: Classification logits for positive, neutral, and negative sentiment; +, 0, and − name labels here.

c, pc.meaning: A selected class and its softmax probability; the three class probabilities sum to 1.

Logit; softmax.meaning: A logit is a raw class score before it is converted to a probability. Softmax turns a group of such scores into shares from 0 to 1 that add to 1, which can be read as estimated class probabilities.

Routing threshold.meaning: Minimum top-class probability required by this classroom workflow before an automatic label is accepted.

FinBERT.meaning: A BERT-based language model adapted to financial text; this hand calculation illustrates attention and classification, not its actual internal parameters.

BERT; transformer.meaning: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) is a language model that uses attention to interpret each word using surrounding words on both sides. This lesson’s small arithmetic example teaches an attention idea; it is not a calculation of BERT’s actual internal settings.

Embedding.meaning: A numerical vector representing text for a similarity comparison; the vectors here are supplied toy values.

q, d.meaning: Query vector and a document-chunk vector, respectively.

q1 , q2 , d1 , d2.meaning: First and second coordinates of the corresponding vectors; subscripts label dimensions.

q·d.meaning: Dot product: sum of products of corresponding coordinates.

∥q∥, ∥d∥.meaning: Euclidean vector lengths, or norms; double bars indicate length, not a confidence score.

sim(q, d).meaning: Cosine similarity; a unitless directional similarity score, not an answer-correctness probability.

Chunk; top two.meaning: A separately indexed passage; the two passages with the highest similarity scores.

RAG.meaning: Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve source material, then use it to support an answer.

R2024 , R2025.meaning: Revenue in the two named years, both in millions of dollars here; R does not mean recall in this exercise.

g, g%.meaning: Fractional growth and its percentage-number form; report g% with a percent sign.

Grounded answer.meaning: An answer whose factual claims can be traced to the supplied evidence or a checked calculation from it.

Parser.meaning: Software that converts a filing into machine-readable text, tables, and structure.

Ntables , Nintact.meaning: Number of audited tables and tables retaining every required header, row, and unit label; eight and seven.

Nrequired , Npresent.meaning: Number of required sections and those appearing in the parsed output; ten and nine.

Ncells , Nwrong.meaning: Audited numeric cells and cells with an incorrect number or unit; 200 and six.

Cell.meaning: One location at the intersection of a table row and column.

Header.meaning: A label explaining what a row or column represents, such as revenue, 2025, or USD millions.

Unit label.meaning: Information specifying the figure’s measurement scale, currency, or other unit; losing it can change the meaning of a correct-looking numeral.

Integrity.meaning: Complete preservation of the specified table elements under this audit rubric, not a general security certification.

Coverage.meaning: Presence of required sections here; a different meaning from automatic-answer coverage or interval coverage.
Observed fraction of evaluated outcomes inside their intervals.

Q, q.meaning: Total question count and one question’s index; four questions are evaluated.
Total number of evaluated questions, here 4, and a question index.

mq.meaning: Number of components required to answer question q fully.

kq.meaning: Number of required components correctly supplied for that question.

1[kq = mq ].meaning: Equals 1 if all required components are supplied correctly; otherwise 0.

Component.meaning: One required fact, calculation, or explanation specified in the answer key.

Rubric.meaning: The explicit criteria used to determine whether an answer contains the required correct content.

Exactness.meaning: Whole-question success rate under this rubric; not exact character matching.

Component completeness.meaning: Correctly supplied required content as a share of all required content, pooled across questions.

Pooled.meaning: Counts are added before division; a question requiring four components contributes four to the component denominator.

w, 1 − w.meaning: Stock and bond weights as fractions of the whole portfolio; together they equal 1.

µs , µb , µp.meaning: Expected annual arithmetic returns for stocks, bonds, and the portfolio; mu denotes a mean here.

σs , σb , σp.meaning: Annual return standard deviations, or volatilities; sigma measures variability, not expected loss.

σp2.meaning: Portfolio variance: squared volatility, in squared decimal-return units.

ρ (rho).meaning: Correlation: how the two assets co-move; assumed to be zero, not estimated in this exercise.

2w(1 − w)ρσs σb.meaning: Covariance contribution to variance; it vanishes under the given zero-correlation assumption.

√.meaning: Square root; converts variance back into the same return units as volatility.

∈, {. . .}.meaning: “Belongs to” and a set of allowed values; the stock weight must be one of the three listed.

V.meaning: Number of alerts requiring review under a threshold: caught fraud plus false alerts.
Portfolio value, $1 million, before transaction costs in the calculation.
Original order value or notional; $1 million here.

Objective.meaning: Quantity to make as small or large as possible; minimize modeled variance here.

Constraint; feasible.meaning: A requirement that must be met; a candidate satisfying every stated requirement.

Optimal candidate.meaning: The best feasible member of the supplied candidate set under these estimates; not a guaranteed outcome.

s, s′.meaning: Current state and next state; the prime marks the state after the action, not a derivative.

a.meaning: An available action, such as buying now or waiting.

Q(s, a).meaning: Estimated discounted cumulative reward from taking action a in state s and continuing thereafter.

Qold , Qnew.meaning: Stored value before and after this learning update.

r.meaning: Immediate reward from the observed action; here negative cost in simulator reward units.

γ (gamma).meaning: Discount factor, 0.9: weight placed on reward one step further into the future.

maxa Q(s′ , a).meaning: Largest estimated value among valid actions in the next state.

T.meaning: Update target; a newly introduced label for immediate plus discounted future reward.
Number of tied-score pairs; this is not time or a tree count here.
Total possible unordered pairs among all six customers: 6 choose 2.
Elapsed queue-building time in seconds; ten minutes equals 600 seconds.
Total scheduled operating minutes in the month; the service is expected to operate 24 hours per day.

δ (delta).meaning: Temporal-difference error: target minus the old action value.

α (alpha).meaning: Learning rate, 0.5: how much of the error is applied to the old estimate.

Greedy policy.meaning: Chooses the action with highest current estimated value; it does not deliberately explore alternatives.

Episode; terminal.meaning: One complete simulated execution task; terminal means that task has ended and no future reward remains.

Q.meaning: Original intended buy quantity, 1,000 shares; not a reinforcement-learning Q-value.

i, qi.meaning: Fill index and quantity bought in that fill; 400 shares in each of two fills.

Pi.meaning: Price paid per share in fill i; $50.10 and $50.20.

P0.meaning: Arrival-price benchmark, $50.00 per share, used for the intended trade’s reference value.

qu.meaning: Shares unfilled by the evaluation endpoint; target quantity minus filled quantities.

Pclose.meaning: Closing price used to value the unfilled-share opportunity cost, $50.30.

F ees.meaning: Total additional execution fees, $20, counted once.

IS.meaning: Implementation shortfall in dollars under the supplied buy-order convention.

V0.meaning: Original target notional: all intended shares valued at the arrival price.

ISbps.meaning: Implementation shortfall as basis points of original target notional; 10,000 basis points equal the whole notional.
